speechtext: Perhaps I may be permitted to explain that this represents one-fifth of the amount of the War Appropriation Bill recently introduced by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. I beg to move that the message from His Royal Highness the Governor General be referred to the Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is not an additional amount; it is only a vote on account of the $250,000,000. It is necessary *to make some provision immediately.. I have explained it to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid L^urier).

speechtext:
My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) has handed me a telegram received from the General Manager of the Intercolonial Railway in regard to return tickets for the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. The telegram is as follows:
Moncton, N.B., 6th April. 1916. Hon. Dr. Reid,
Ottawa, Ont.
Yours 5th re transportation of soldiers. I assume this refers to officers and men of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces. The Canadian Government railways grant the same privilege as applies over all other railways in Canada, namely, on presentation of militia certificate officers and men are granted round trip tickets at first-class fare and one-third. Mailing you to-day copy of our fare notice number 217.
F. P. Gutelius.
That is the regulation in force at the present time. Possibly my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) had in mind something beyond that.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to correct a
statement which I made the other day in the House concerning Japanese immigration. In connection with a return of the Department of Trade and Commerce, during the discussion of the Estimates of that department, I stated that Japanese immigrants had come to Canada in very great numbers of late. On looking up the monthly statement I find that I made a mistake. I should have said that Japanese immigration, due to the war conditions prevailing both here and in Japan, had decreased; in fact, last year the decrease in immigration amounted to 419.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY-SNOW BLOCKADE ON ESTEVAN-CARLYLE LINE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY-SNOW BLOCKADE ON ESTEVAN-CARLYLE LINE.
speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the Government and of the hon. Acting Minister of Railways and Canals to the following telegram which I received this morning:
Esteven, Sask., April 6.
J. G. Turriff, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Canadian Northern line Estevan Carlyle blocked for several weeks and no effort being made to relieve serious situation; Lampman and other points out of coal; severe weather still prevails; please use your good offices to get line opened.
(Sgd.) Estevan Board of Trade.
There should not be much excuse, for no efforts having been made to open that line, because I brought this matter to the attention of the House repeatedly over two months ago, when the condition was very bad. The people had at that time been 25 days without 'a train and were suffering from lack of coal and food. This line connects with the main line from Winnipeg to Regina, and there should riot be any great difficulty in getting it opened.
The other railways in that part of the country have been running all winter. Four days is the longest tie-up at one time on any of them. So there i^ very little excuse for this condition of affairs. I brought this matter to the attention of the chairman of the Railway Commission this morning. They had advice of it, but not enough was done by the railway company. The acting Minister of Railways should get after the railway company, and see that they give some sort of accommodation to the settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
maintopic: CANADIAN NORTHERN RAILWAY-SNOW BLOCKADE ON ESTEVAN-CARLYLE LINE.
speechtext:
I will bring the matter to the attention of the Railway Commission, which the hon. gentleman knows is the only body that has authority to deal with matters of this kind. The Minister of Railways can only work through that board, in order to bring about any action that may be necessary. When the hon. member brought this matter to the attention of the House on a former occasion, information was given to him that everything that could be done by the railway itself and the Board of Railway Commissioners was being
done. The telegram he has read states that at present there is very severe weather in that part of the country, which is ho doubt the reason they cannot get the road open. I have the greatest confidence in Sir Henry Drayton and his fellow commissioners, and believe they will do everything possible to keep open every road in the country.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to draw your attention to an error in the Hansard report of the sitting of the 2nd of March. On that day there was a discussion on the Estimates between the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) and the Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) regarding a certain correspondence which was alleged to have passed between the Minister of Militia and high officials in the Conservative party in Regina. The Minister of Militia is reported to have spoken in this way:
Sir Sam Hughes: There was no quarrel between that gentleman and myself as to who should dictate the patronage. The trouble was that I found something not exactly square, and I did not care whether he was Grit or Tory, i his head came off.
I was not present at the discussion, but I am informed that certain words of the Minister of Militia were not reported. My information is to this effect that the minister said:
There was no quarrel between that gentleman and myself as to who should dictate the patronage.
The words omitted were: " I found that fellow grafting, and "- Then followed the words at the end of the sentence:	" his
head came off." But, as I have read, the1 report in'Hansard continues, after the word " patronage ":
I found something not exactly square, and 1 did not care whether he was Grit or Tory, his head came off.
But, as I am informed, the words which the minister used were:	" I found that
fellow grafting." The reason why I bring the matter to the attention of the House is that the words have been reported in some newspapers as they are alleged to have been spoken, and as I have just quoted. They were so reported in the Globe, and the report in the Globe was copied in the Leader, of Regina. A suit for libel is taken against the Leader, and therefore it becomes important that the exact truth should be known, and that,

if the words were spoken as alleged, the Hansard report should be corrected. Personally, I know nothing of the matter. The reports of Hansard are generally very fair and very correct; I have no complaint to make and do not think that anybody will make complaint. But sometimes errors will creep in; and, in this case, if I am correctly informed, there has certainly been an omission. I am told that if you, Mr. Speaker, will call the attention of the reporters to the matter, a correction will be made. Therefore I ask that the matter be rectified.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should think it undesirable that the House should interfere in a matter pending in the courts, unless the case is absolutely plain. At all events, if any action is to be taken, it should be brought up, in the first instance, in the Debates Committee, which has special charge of such matters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have no objection that the matter should be considered by the Debates Committee. I think that a very proper course.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to call attention to a provision contained in the Act of 1914, relating to the Canadian Northern railway. I do so because there have been a good many complaints during this session concerning the operation of the line. I refer to Chapter 20 of the Statutes of 1914, section 16, which authorizes the Governor in Council to appoint a director of the Canadian Northern. I desire to ask if the director has been appointed, and, if so, the name of that director.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Finance informs me that the director has not been appointed; that is his impression at the moment. We will ascertain precisely. I have no recollection of the matter having come before the Government.
The hon. gentleman is aware of the section I have referred to, authorizing the appointment of a director by the Governor in Council?

speechtext:
Yes. ENLISTMENT OF EDWARD PAQUETTE.
On the Orders of the Day:

I would remind the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence of the re-

marks I made last week with regard to a young man who was being enlisted without the authority of his father. I have not had any answer from the acting minister on the subject yet, but I am obliged to the hon. gentleman, -for I received a letter from the father that the 'boy has been sent back.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext: It was not necessary for me to give a further statement; because I gave instructions that the hoy should be returned, the officer wired me that my instructions would toe carried out, and afterwards wired me that the hoy had been returned.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: WAR SUPPLIES - PETROLEUM FOR MUNITION WORKS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: WAR SUPPLIES - PETROLEUM FOR MUNITION WORKS.
speechtext:
I desire to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals and of the Acting Minister of Militia to a letter which the Imperial Oil Company has written to the Lachine Manufacturing Company concerning the transportation of petroleum. The letter is as follows:
Toronto, Ont., 31st March, 1916. Messrs. La Cie ManufacturiSre de Lachine, Lachine, Qu6.
Dear Sirs,-We desire to call your attention to the fact that both the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway have issued embargoes, which have the effect of prohibiting shipments of petroleum and its products to you.
Therefore, we believe it is absolutely necessary, in order to prevent the serious condition which is bound to occur if you do not receive promptly shipments of petroleum and its products, which you use in the manufacture of war materials, to take up with the Minister of Militia and advise him as to how serious this action on the part of the railroads is going to effect the manufacture and deliveries by you of such war materials and request that he should issue such instructions to the railroads as will compel them to make an exception of petroleum and its products in all their embargoes.
We have felt that the situation as existing today on the railroads is so serious that, unless we have your co-operation, there is no way to predict what the result will be.
Tours truly,
(Sgd.) The Imperial Oil Company, Limited.
I only ask if the hon. ministers will cooperate in an endeavour to find a remedy for that situation.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
maintopic: WAR SUPPLIES - PETROLEUM FOR MUNITION WORKS.
speechtext:
On account of the very large amount of traffic which is being moved throughout the country at the present time, the railroads find it necessary occasionally to put an embargo upon certain commodi-

ties. The embargo upon crude oil and petroleum was put on a short time ago; and, on the representations of several manufacturers that they would have to close down their businesses if this embargo were continued, I made representations to the Railway Commission. I have since been informed, both verbally and by letter, that this embargo has been removed and that the traffic is again moving as usual.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I notice in the press a report emanating from Winnipeg that the Government has decided To allow the alien prisoners in Western Canada to be utilized as farm labourers during the spring season. I would like to ask the Government, if that statement is correct, under what circumstances the men are to be placed and how they are to be guarded while they are employed on the farms.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
This question has been
taken up, and General Otter has left for Winnipeg to consult with the commandants of the different internment camps, with a view to making suitable arrangements for the release of the prisoners to assist in the planting of the crop. His purpose in going to Winnipeg is to facilitate means by which this work can be carried out in a manner satisfactory to his department and to the people of Western Canada.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 74, to Levy a Tax on Business Profits.-Sir Thomas White. Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 6-computation of profits:

Would the minister
state in a general way how he expects to arrive at the amount of taxation due? Will he endeavour to arrive at it from the reports sent in by the various companies who are either liable or likely to be liable under this measure, or by sending out officials to visit the different companies and assessing the amount of the levy at the head office of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the first instance, returns will be called for under the provisions of the Act. Those returns will be examined, and, if necessary, a further investigation made into them; and the assessments will be made subsequently.
If the return looks in a general way to be satisfactory, the amount will be arrived at, at the head office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the return appears to be correct-so far as we can check it up, it will be accepted. Of course, we have mercantile agencies' reports which will enable us to form an idea as to whether the return is substantially correct or not.

I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that the figures which would be given under the forms set out at the end of the Bill would not prove anything. In the form to be used by incorporated companies there is no column for total liabilities, whereas there is such a column in the form to be, used Iby persons other than incorporated companies. In the form to be used by incorporaed companies there is a column for cost of management, etc., whereas in that for non-incorporated companies there is no such column. I think that .some incorporated companies would have great difficulty in preparing a statement showing the cost of management, etc. I have in mind an incorporated company which has several branches, and the cost of management of each branch is charged up to that branch monthly or perhaps daily. It is evident that the cost of management in this case would Ibe very hard to get at. The company that I have in mind has. been asked several times by its bankers to supply such information, but it has been practically impossible for them to do .so; at any rate, they did not think it was practicable for them to try to furnish that information. Their statements are prepared along the line of the schedule in this Bill in Tespect of partnership companies. The total assets and total liabilities are shown, and the subtraction of one from the other shows the capital and surplus. The figures required by these statements are taken from the balance sheet of the company for that accounting period, and it is necessary to show the total liabilities and total assets in order to ascertain the capital and surplus. Another difficulty that will present itself is that some companies may have $30,000 or $40,000 worth of dry goods in stock, some of which may have been on the shelves for seven or eight yeaTS and may have depreciated very much in value. But the management, instead of going over the stock and putting the actual value on the goods, say to the employees: Put this stock down at cost price. I do not know whether or not the

minister 'has considered the advisability of making an allowance for depreciation in such cases. In the large wholesale houses if a piece of goods depreciates in value the proper value is put on that piece of goods, but that is not done in the retail business. Then, subsection 2 says:
The profits of a non-Canadian company shall be the net profits arising from its Canadian business including both domestic and export business.
The Armour Company at Hamilton do a large Canadian 'business as well as a large business arising from their Chicago house. For instance, they sell large quantities of soap in Canada, and they sell also large quantities of packing house products direct from Chicago. Would the minister consider any profits arising from that portion of the business of Armour and -Company to be Canadian business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend certain that the 'business is carried on under the name of Armour and Company in Hamilton, or is it under special incorporation? If it is under special incorporation that incorporation would, be dealt with as a Canadian company. If the American house to which my hon. friend has reference has no domicile in Canada, but sells in Canada from outside, it would not be within the power of the Dominion to reach them by direct taxation.

I think each of the
branches of this company is domiciled, if you like, under a separate name. There is the original Armour and Company; there is the soap company. The name of the one in Hamilton, I think, is the Armour-Fowler Company; at any rate, they succeeded Fowler. They are all branches of the same company, Armour and Company, the large packers of Chicago. What does the minister say as to my suggestion with regard to allowance for depreciation of stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There should be an allowance for depreciated stock if depreciation can be established as a fact. It is a question of good usage in a particular trade or business. With regard to the second schedule, to which my hon. friend has referred, I purpose taking out the words "cost of management, etc." I think that "gross profits" and "net profits" will be quite sufficient.
That would be an improvement, I think.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 7-capital of a company:

Has the minister thought of the fact that there may be companies with their head offices in, for example, the United States or Great Britain, that are doing a large business in Canada and have really no assets in Canada? Shipping companies might have ships registered in Great Britain; they would have offices in Montreal, or some other Canadian city, and carry on a large business and make large profits in Canada. Does the minister expect to get any revenue from companies of that character?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have assets, then the capital employed would be ascertained under the provisions of subsection 2. If they have no assets in Canada I know of no means whereby our legislation could reach them. They would net be within the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government.
I thought, perhaps, the minister had some method of getting at their profits so as to obtain taxation on their Canadian business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of British companies, we need have no anxiety as to their paying their share of war taxation, because the Imperial Finance Act No. 2, and the recent Budget of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, impose very heavy burdens on such companies. I have been amazed at the amounts levied on Canadian companies under Finance Act No. 2, which was passed last December. The amounts are very much larger than any taxation we propose.
I assume the minister has adopted the theory that the place of registry of a ship is the place of its ownership, and, that if a ship is not registered in Canada it is not a Canadian, asset.*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While that is a legal question on which I am not quite certain, I think the place of registry would be the domicile of the ship.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-boards of referees:
What powers does Part I. of the Inquiries Act give?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have the power to exercise judicial functions, to send for witnesses and take evidence, and generally adjudicate on the matter under consideration.
What will be the area over which each board will have jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not fully determined that, but I think it would make for the convenience of the public if there were a board for each province, or at least for each section of the country, if the country could be divided into sections. I think it would be the object of the Government to provide sufficient boards to ensure the prompt hearing of appeals against assessments. My present view is that there should be a board for each province, but it may be found that a board of reference may be able to serve more than one province.
Will the commissioners be paid by salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should think not; an allowance of so much per day would probably cover the case.

Has the minister in mind any class from which he will select the members of the board? I have had suggestions made to me by business men in my own province that it would be undesirable to appoint business men to the position. I suppose that,the objectors think that if men in general mercantile business were appointed, in a small province, they would obtain a knowledge of other people's business which would not be desirable. There might be something in the practice in Ontario where county court judges are not appointed for the district in which they have practised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We certainly desire to have boards composed of men of ability and standing and absolute fairness; in other words, high-class men.
And men who are not known as extreme party followers. If they are high-class men, of course they will not be affected by partisanship.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think there are any extreme partisans in Canada now, in the midst of the war?
I imagine many will present themselves for appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It being a business tax, I see the force of the suggestion of my hon. friend, and possibly it might be well to have members of the legal profession or county court judges. I shall give the matter very careful consideration. Certainly my own intention is to appoint high-class men, who will deal with absolute fairness with all appeals coming before them; because they will be exercising judicial functions, and the rights of the public must be protected.

I would like to protest
against the minister's last suggestion, that they may be lawyers or judges. No county court judge whom I know knows any more about a business statement than a hen knows about holy water. The great mass of lawyers know nothing about business statements. There may be some lawyers who know something about business, but very few, according to my knowledge.
Order.
Is my hon. friend not aware that most business statements are made by lawyers?

So far as my section of
the country is concerned, no lawyer makes any business statement that I know of; the business men make the statements them-iselves. I think that the referees should be business men. I do not think that because they know something about the other man's business they would peddle. I will endorse my hon. friend's suggestion that partnership should be kept out as much as possible; but, whether manufacturers, commercial men, or accountants, the referees should certainly be business men who understand the compiling of business statements.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-return required, partnerships, etc.; enlarging time:

I suppose that
under section 10 the liability is imposed upon every person liable to be taxed to deliver a return without notice. I assume that the department will in some way endeavour to send out some notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The statute must take this form in order to create the obligation, but we shall have complete lists made and copies of the Act sent out with the forms to be filled in and returned.
Does this section or any following section follow the English Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed'
that in all our provincial legislation the taxation of companies is administered in the first instance by requiring a form 'to

be filled in. Afterwards, of 4 p.m. course, the department may make such inquiries as are deemed necessary before making the final assessment. I am not able to say off-hand whether this follows the English form or not.

Will the minister send out any instructions ih connection with this schedule, or will this schedule alone be sent out? It is a very meagre document, and it strikes me that it would be well to issue some instructions. There may be many people who think that they are not taxable at all under this Bill, and who have an idea that the value of their property does not amount to $50,000. I think the minister should lay down some rules by which people would be guided, and .send them out along with the schedules that have to be filled in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the intention to send to each parity who is thought to be liable to assessment, a copy of the Act, a circular letter, and the form to be filled up.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section II-Minister may request further return, production of books, etc:
iMr. A. K. MACLEAN: The board makes' the assessment in each case, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The department makes the assessment, and if anybody is dissatisfied with the assessment he can appeal to the board of referees.
Then the board is merely-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A court of revision.

In the schedule it is provided that the information under the headings of "Values of assets outside Canada" and "Profits of Canadian business" will be required only from companies having their head office or other place of business outside Canada. It appears to me that there should be some provision -whereby we could get at the insurance companies who have their head offices outside, of Canada, but who are doing business in Canada, such as the mutual companies in the Eastern States, which do a very large business here, and do it at a much cheaper rate than our own companies or the English companies can. I understand that they

are not taxed under this Bill and that they are not get-at-able.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not get-at-able.

Is it not unfair that they should escape? Why should they escape whilst they are taking profits from this country. Is there not some method whereby the profits which they obtain by way of premiums could be taxed? Why can it not be worked out the same as in the case of other companies? The letter sent out by the Canada Fire Insurance Federation, St. James Street, Montreal, has no doubt come to the minister's attention. It appears to me that the arguments set out there are fair, and, looking at the matter purely from a layman's standpoint, I think that if these companies are doing business in Canada, making profits out of the people of Canada, a case should be made out against them, particularly seeing that our own companies are to be taxed. I should like to have an explanation from the minister as to whether it would not be possible to tax the profits of those outside companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This matter was discussed last night when my hon. friend was not in the House. This Bill could not be made to apply to those companies because they are not domiciled in Canada, and have no offices in Canada. They are for the most part, New Epgland mutual companies. Even if they had offices here, it is not probable that they would be liable to assessment under this Bill, because being mutual companies they would not have profits. The question is not a new one, it is an old one, and it has been suggested that as the Dominion Government has no power to directly tait those companies, domiciled, as they are, outside of Canada, a tax should be imposed upon the premiums which are paid by the parties in Canada who take out policies of insurance with such companies.
It is recognized that the Dominion cannot reach them directly and it is suggested that they should be reached indirectly by a direct tax upon the insurers here, that is to say, upon the manufacturers and business people generally throughout the country who place insurance with these unlicensed companies. As I pointed out last night when the matter was up in 1910, there was an acute controversy about it. My predecessor was unable to deal with it. A Bill providing for a tax upon the premiums on insurance policies placed with these

companies was passed by the House of Commons but was rejected 'by the Senate. So, the matter is one of acute controversy between the insurers on the one hand and the insurance companies on the other. It would not be possible, under the provisions of this Bill, to deal with the case. As I said last night, there is no doubt a good deal to be said in favour of the position which the insurance companies of Canada ta'ke. They say: We pay a license fee to do business in Canada and we are taxed in Canada; why should we not be protected against the unlicensed companies which take out no licenses, and pay no taxes in Canada?
The minister says that under this Bill it is impossible to get at these companies. When we are imposing war taxes, is not this the very time to get at them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You cannot get at these companies. This is a tax upon the business profits of companies doing business in Canada. These other companies have no domicile in Canada and therefore it is impossible to apply this Bill to them. The only way would be by a supplementary measure of taxation taxing the premiums paid by the insurers throughout Canada. Most business people throughout Canada will be taxed specially by this measure. To impose another tax upon them would be to impose an additional measure of taxation. My own view is that this matter should .be dealt with upon a revision of the Insurance Act. If the contention is sound to-day, and there is much to toe said for it, that taxation should be levied tipon insurers in Canada, that was true two years ago, it was true five years ago, it was true before the outbreak of the war and it will be true after the war is concluded. That question is not necessarily connected with the question of taxation now any more than it was with the licensing and taxing of companies before this war broke out. We have brought down this measure of taxation and it is not the intention of the Government to bring down an additional measure of taxation this year. I do not propose to 'bring down an additional Budget. The time to consider it is when the Insurance Act is under revision.

I rather take issue with
the minister upon that. I think the proper time to consider it is now, when you are making extraordinary efforts to raise money
by taxation schemes. If that is so, surely it is not necessary to leave out the people who are making their profits in Canada. It would not be necessary to further tax the insurer; it would only be necessary to say to those companies: if you are to do business in Canada we demand a portion of the profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend, I think, misunderstands the situation. How are we going to say to these insurance companies: you must pay us a certain amount of money? The only way we can meet the situation is by taxing A, B, and C by a supplementary measure of taxation, in respect to the insurance that they have taken out in these companies. The burden would not fall upon the companies, but upon the insurer. That is the point.

I was going to
suggest to the minister that clause 9, which refers to the establishment of a board of referees, is hardly in its proper place. I think it should be just preceding section 15 and under "Assessment Appeals." Section 9 indicates that a board shall be established, but there is no way of knowing its powers or duties until you get ahead to section 15.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it necessary to change it.

What period does the
return asked for after the first of July cover? Does it cover the year 1915?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The accounting
period which terminates after the first of January, 1915.

Is there any way of getting at the profits of the large American grain dealers who deal on the Toronto and Winnipeg grain exchanges, more especially Winnipeg, such as the Armours, Patten and that class of people, and who are supposed to make large profits? They "hedge" on grain-anybody who understands grain exchange business will know what that means -and they make very large profits in the transfer from month to month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If they are carrying on business in grain in Canada, and if

they have capital invested in that business, they will be liable if their profits are such as to bring them within the provisions of the Act. A grain firm might have very small offices and yet might have a good deal of money invested in the business in Canada.
I do not think they are capitalized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They might have a good deal of money invested in carrying this grain and otherwise in connection with the conduct of their business. In the case of an American firm doing business in Canada from the United States, its capital might relate to its American business and not to its Canadian business and, if so, the Act would not apply.

I think they all have
branch offices in Toronto or Winnipeg, especially Winnipeg. They do not carry capital, I think, but they have a large amount of money invested and the minister might get at them in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that would be capital.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 12-penalty for not making return and for false statement:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move that the words " next " and " to " in the second line be transposed.
Section amended as proposed, agreed to.
On section 13-assessment by minister; payment of taxes where two accounting periods accrue on 1st July, 1916; liability to pay tax continued for three years:

I would suggest that we take this up clause by clause; it is too involved to follow by merely reading. I would like to have an explanation of the first clause. What is the purpose and effect of this provision with regard to two accounting periods in one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall that when the measure was first introduced it was pointed out that there might be taxation payments in respect to two accounting payments falling due in the present year, and in order to relieve taxpayers from having to make payment in respect of both we determined to spread the payments over three years.
Will the hon. minister please take a case; we can follow it much better.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Take the case of a firm whose accounting periocL ended 31st January, 1915. Its next accounting period would end 31st January, 1916. Now, if we made the assessment in respect of those two accounting periods this year the firm in question would have to pay, in 1916, the taxation in respect of 'both accounting periods. So the following proviso is made:
Provided, however, that if on the first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen, any person is liable to pay a tax for two or more accounting periods, comprising a period of not less than two years, then such person may pay the tax for the accounting period or periods comprised' in the first twelve months on the first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and sixteen, and for the accounting period or periods comprised in the second twelve months, on the first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and seventeen, and may pay a tax for the accounting period or periods comprised in the subsequent twelve months on the first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen.
So the parties assessed will be liable to pay on only one accounting period in twelve months.

The Bill provides:
In default of payment, interest at the rate of ten per centum per annum shall be paid on such tax until the said tax and interest are paid.
Is this ten per cent in the nature of a penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes,

Does that apply to the poor fellow whose accounting periodt ends, as the minister has said, on the 31st of January, 1915, and then has another on the 31st of January, 1916, and postpones payment until next year? Does the ten per cent apply to the postponement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, for he is not in default. This is in the nature of a penalty. Otherwise, there might be difficulty in collecting it.

The minister allows postponement of payment for the second accounting period for the very purpose of assisting the man to pay. It is almost certain that the only reason a man does not pay when the tax is due is that he is too hard up. Don't you think that ten per cent is a rather severe penalty? Would not seven per cent be quite enough? A tax is not like any other debt; the man will pay

it promptly if he possibly can. And you do not help him to pay by adding ten per cent to his tax. I have always argued for that principle as against people who, when a man is 'behind in his payments, impose an excessive penalty. I think it is a mistake; for, if a man is honest and willing to pay, nothing is gained by adding excessive interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This penalty is in most assessment measures. My view is that the parties who will be liable to this tax will 'be so well able to pay that there will probably not be much in arrear. But I have no objection to reducing it to seven per cent, and; probably that is sufficient. I move:
That in the twenty-eighth line of subsection 1, the word " ten " be struck out and the word " seven " substituted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
If a man makes no return for three years, as mentioned under subsection 3, will he have to pay interest.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The assessment
would have to be made, and then, if he failed to pay at the time that the payment became due, the interest penalty would apply.
If he did not appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I say that the
assessment would be made. By " assessment " I mean, if appealed against, the assessment as revised or confirmed by the court.
Subsection 3 seems to be more in accord with the Statute of Limitations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is the word "for" in line 35 correct? The line reads: "to be paid by any person for the tax." Should not that be " to be paid by any person as the tax"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it would be better phraseology to say " the amount of the tax to be paid by any person." I therefore move:
That subsection 2 be amended by inserting the words " of the tax " after the word " amount " in line 34, and by striking out the words "for the tax " in line 35.
Subsection 2 will then read:
The minister shall not be bound by any return or information supplied by or on behalf of a taxpayer, and, notwithstanding such return of information, or if no return has been made, the minister may determine the amount of the tax to be paid by any person.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Subsection 4 gives the minister power to distribute the assessment between the original owner and the subsequent owner?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
But it does not give him power to distrain on the goods, and the owner may be worthless.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is the best you can do under the circumstances referred to.

The person who sells
out may not be worth while taxing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he has sold out, the goods are gone.

Not necessarily. I may
sell out to the Chairman, but my goods are still in the business which the Chairman carries on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But he may have sold them by the time the assessment can be made.
I do not think subsection 4 is a very good one. It is the person who endeavours to evade the tax that we want to make pay.
Is there any provision in the Bill for establishing a lien?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is further on in the Bill.

Subsection 4 says, in part:
The minister may, if-he thinks fit, take the accounting period as the period ending on the date on which the ownership has so changed and assess the tax on the person who owned or carried on the business or acted as agent for the person carrying on the business at that date.
As I understand it, he does not take the right to levy the tax on the business itself, no matter who may be carrying it on. If he did so, the person who purchased would be very careful to see that he had deducted the amount that was liable for the tax from the purchase price, as is usually done in a transfer of real estate.
As long as a tax is a lien, I do not think that sub-section will be used very much. Of course, there might be no property in many eases.

Would it be -worth while to have the referees for the different provinces make a return to, say, the county court clerks, showing that the taxes had been paid? In that way, in the case of a transfer of business, one could search in order to see whether the tax had been paid or not.
Section 22 also levies the tax only against the person. I do not believe that subsection 4 is a good one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It meets the case of a party who has been carrying on business for, let us .say, a portion of a year, and sells out to another party. Two questions would arise: First, as to who could be assessed; and, secondly, as to whether there was a true accounting period which would come under the provisions of the Act relating to the accounting period. Power is taken by this subsection for the minister to take the accounting period as the period ending on the date the ownership .so changed, so that the assessment could be made against that person on the, so to speak, broken accounting period. This subsection follows the precise wording of the English Act, and I think it is the .best that can be done to meet the situation, in question. No doubt there will be cases in which men will sell out and go away, and in which the Dominion Government will not be able to tax. That happens in connection, with all assessments. Take the old personal property asessment in the municipalities in .Ontario. In a considerable .percentage of cases it was not possible to levy the tax because of changes that have taken place.

In Ontario your goods are liable for the tax, no matter whether you have incurred the payment or not. If taxes .are due on a certain house and if I move into that house, my goods are liable for the tax and .can 'he seized. That is the point I want to bring out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not see that we can change the section. I think the real safeguard is the fact that we are dealing with businesses that have capital of at least $50,006-with a class of people that are likely to pay up and not evade taxation.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 15-court of revision:
What does the minister say to my suggestion of bringing section 9 forward? I think it is misplaced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bill will be reprinted for the third reading, and can be recast in that respect. I suppose no objection will he taken to that being done on the third reading.
This Bill will be read considerably, and you have to go to clause 15 before you find out the duties of the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that the suggestion is a good one. .
Do we understand that the board is simply a court of revision and appeal, which 'has nothing to do with the making of assessment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The court of revision has power, once the appeal is taken, to make the assessment, but a board of referees does not initiate the assessment in any way. It is a court of appeal, with power to hear evidence, adjudicate upon such evidence, and confirm or amend the assessment.
Return is made direct to the minister, not to the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 16-notice of appeal.
Can one taxpayer appeal from the assessment levied against another?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I have not made that provision. I gave it some thought, but I thought it inexpedient in connection with Dominion taxation. A good deal is to be said for it in connection with provincial taxation, but we are following the precedent of the Customs Act, which provides that only parties in interest can bring a matter of customs valuation before the Customs Board.
Is twenty days sufficient notice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We thought it was, having regard to the size of the country. There is a proviso re special cases:
Provided, however, that the minister, either before or after the expiry of the said twenty days, may give a taxpayer further time in which to appeal.

I think you ought to
make it thirty days. Thirty days go by very quickly when you give a note, you know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think twenty days is ample. I move that the word " sixteen " in line 30 of section 16 be struck out, and that the word " thirteen " be substituted therefor.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 17-hearing and decision by board:
If an appeal is successful, does the department pay the costs of the appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The costs would be, I think, in the discretion of the court. I should have to consider that and let it stand for the third reading. It is not usual, I think, to provide for payment of costs by the Crown unless the court so directs.
It seems hardly fair that the appellant should in any event have to pay the costs, even if successful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
does not mean "in any event "; he means in the event of being successful.

He would naturally pay
them if unsuccessful, but it seems hardly fair that he should pay them if successful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
realizes that provision for the payment of costs might put a premium, so to speak, upon litigating questions of taxation.

Line 4 of this section reads:	" The board may in any case
before it increase the assessment." This wording neither looks nor sounds correct. How would it do to make it read:	" The
board may increase the assessment in any case before it "?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think
that that would be an improvement; I think it is perfectly clear as it stands.

This does not seem to
me to be an ordinary equity suit. The value has been given by one party, and you are suing for it, and if you are not successful you may have a right to pay the costs. Inasmuch as the Government are asking a share of the profits of the firm in question, if there be a dispute as to the amount of these ptofits, and it is carried to a board, and the board decides against the owner of the business, it seems rather drastic to call upon him to pay the costs. The Government should pay all costs. They have the
machinery for levying the tax, they have their board appointed in a regular way, and why Exchequer Court fees should be added is something beyond me.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like to go as far as my hon. friend suggests, because that means that, whether the appeal is successful or not, the Crown would have to pay the costs. That would really put a premium on appeals and would be too good a thing for the lawyers. I have an amendment which I think will meet the situation. I move that subsection 2 be amended by adding after the last word, " appeals," the following, " and if an appeal is successful the board may recommend that the costs be paid by the Crown." That is the language used with respect to costs which may be payable by the Crown.

The issue to be determined by the board might be whether or not a certain amount fixed by the minister was the correct amount; and a further question might be involved as to whether the amount that was asserted by the party who was taxed was the correct amount. Then the issue might be whether there was any right to tax at all. The words " if the appeal is successful " seem to me to bo hardly applicable.

It might well be that
the party might succeed on one point and fail on another, and it is possible that the most equitable way to deal with it would be to put it in the discretion of the board to determine how the cost should be paid.t If we assert the right, we should have it' the same on both sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think an appeal would be on the question of whether there was liability at all, or else as to the amount of liability. The appeal would be successful if the appellant established that he was not liable, and the appeal would also be successful if the assessment, as the result of the appeal, was reduced. It would seem to me that the word " successful " would cover both cases, but if my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) will think the phrasing over before the third reading, I shall be glad to have a more apt phraseology suggested.

It might be that to establish that he was not liable to taxation the appellant would have to go to a great deal of expense in the way of accounting and so on, and it would seem only fair that the Crown should be liable for his costs.

Section 16 provides
two forms of appeal. We have the case of a person objecting to the amount for which he is assessed, and the case of a person claiming to have been wrongfully assessed. The form K would apply, I suppose, to the first of those two classes of cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that I withdraw the amendment?

Let it stand, and look at it.
Section 17 and proposed amendment stand.
On section 18-proceeding ex parte:
Is there any clause which fixes the place where the hearing of an appeal by the referees shall take place? I think the place should be limited to the province in which the party is situated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under section 15 the board "shall hear and determine any appeal made by a taxpayer under this Act in such place in Canada as the minister may direct." We do not know at the present time how many boards it will be necessary to establish, and after determining that it is the intention to create the boards and specify the places at which they shall sit for the purpose of hearing appeals.

I think it is very important that facilities should be given for an appeal to be heard in the locality where the business is carried on; otherwise it would be oppressive if a man had to take a trip and carry his books into another province. There is a clause which enables the minister to make regulations, and I think that would be a proper matter to be dealt with in the minister's regulations. I do not see why an appellant should not have the right to trial in the county in which he has his business.
Section 18 agreed to.
On section 19-appeal to Exchequer Court:

I would suggest that that part of this clause which provides that the taxpayer may appeal within ten days after the mailing of the decision should be amended so as to read that his right to appeal shall be within ten days after the receipt of the decision. To limit the time within which one must appeal by the mail-

ing of the notice is an unusual thing. In some cases it might take ten days to reach the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The trouble is that he might never get it.

How is the taxpayer to know when it was mailed? He might know it by looking at the envelope, which might disclose the mailing date, but frequently it does not. Why not say 15 days after the decision of the Board; per-
5 p.m. haps that would be sufficient.
No doubt the taxpayer would be reading the proceedings of the Board. Make it 15 days after the decision, and require that the decision be mailed to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do require that the decision be mailed to him. If it were made 15 days after the decision, I think that would cover the case.

The statute must provide for some legal notice. Throw a duty upon the referees board to send a registered letter to the party, then prima facie he has notice, and he can easily satisfy the proper tribunal that he had never received that notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: While the matter presents some difficulty, I think that the date of mailing should be the date, because, under decisions, if I send a letter to an individual, that letter is deemed to be his letter from the time it goes into the post office. But, in order to prevent any hardship upon appellants, I would move that the word "ten" in line 17 be struck out, and the word "twenty" substituted therefor.
Should the letter not be registered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has to be registered.
Section 19, amended as proposed, agreed to.
On section 20-exclusive jurisdiction of Exchequer Court:
That means an appeal from the Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
An appeal
or certiorari etc., from the Board.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.'
On section 23-recovery of tax, interest, costs, or penalty:	.
Who gets the penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be for the use of His Majesty.

This clause does not give the Exchequer Court power to grant costs. I do not think it would be a power that would be inherent in the Exchequer Court under this classification. It is purely a statutory court.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend suggests that the Exchequer Court will not have jurisdiction over the matter of costs unless the power is expressly given?
I do not think so.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) raised the question as to whether express power should be given to the Exchequer Court to impose costs. It would appear to me that the court would have that power by reason of its jurisdiction. If there is any doubt, it might be well to make it clear.
Section 17, subsection 2, says that "the tariff of fees in force in the Exchequer Court of Canada shall apply to such appeals." You might adopt the word " costs."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In order to meet the case in point I move that section 20 be reconsidered, and that it be amended by adding thereto. " and may award costs in connection therewith." That leaves it to the discretion of the court.
To make this more general, we might say that the court shall have the same discretionary power to deal with the question of costs as it has in all other matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that the words " and may award costs in connection therewith " will cover the case.

Yes, I think that
will be all right.
On the third reading you may amend the phraseology if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we read the Bill a third5 time I will call attention to it. This is an important measure, and we will try to amend in it any defects of phraseology.

In order to be absolutely certain about it, we would need to look at the Exchequer Court Act.
167*

The phraseology does not seem to me to be right. I think it should be, " and may determine the question of costs." It is all right to let it go that way, but I would suggest that when the Bill is reprinted it be changed.
Section, amended as proposed, agreed to.

Does not the minister think that to apply Exchequer Court costs *to such proceedings as these is to impose very excessive costs? The cost of proceedings in the Exchequer Court frightens the ordinary man. An individual or firm would suffer a considerable amount of hardship rather than go into the Exchequer Court.
Oh, no.
I differ from my hon. friend on that point. From my standpoint I think it is decidedly objectionable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to dispose of section 17, I beg to move:
That section 17 be reconsidered and that all the words after the word " costs " in line 9 be stricken out and the following be substituted therefor: " or part of the costs of such appeal, and if such appeal is successful the board may recommend that the costs, or any part thereof, be paid by the Crown."
Section, amended as proposed, agreed to.
On section 24-tax, etc., first lien.

I suppose that lien
takes priority of bonds, wages of employees, and all other claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has asked a difficult legal question, and I can hardly say in advance what the courts will hold. The intention of the section is to give a lien for the taxation.

If it is a lien, it should be registered in the province. Take the ease of a person doing business with a firm against whom the lien could be asserted; unless there were registration, his creditors would have no notice of the lien, and that would not be fair to them. There could be no objection to the Crown registering its lien.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think there will be great inconvenience in registering. A municipality taxes real 'and personal property, and has a lien, and yet there is no registration. If the purchaser of property-desires to make a search, he goes to the treasurer of the municipality or the taxation officer. In the same way, every one

has notice of this taxation, and, if he desires to make a search, inquiry can be made of the Dominion Government.

But all that ds needed is that the officials of the department should give notice of the claim for registration. I cannot see where the inconvenience would come in. And the registration would he only a reasonable protection to creditors, which might be extremely important in the case of those dealing with firms liable to the tax that may be in financial difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know any provincial machinery that would enable us to file these liens. In what provincial office is provision made for the filing of a Dominion lien? Not only would there be inconvenience in filing, but I feel that it would be impossible to file such liens as this against properties throughout the Dominion, because the machinery for it does not exist.	.
I do not see more difficulty in the case of the Dominion Government filing any lien than in the case of anybody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where should we file :t?

In the registration office of the district. In every province, title to real estate is recorded in the registry office. Bona fide creditors could go and make inquiry as to whether the taxes were paid or not. Is it intended to assert that this shall be a first lien, ahead of a mortgage, a judgment in the hands of the sheriff, or other lien of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The intention is to give a lien, but whether the Dominion lien would prevail over a first lien given under the law of the province is a question that I am not able to determine offhand, and I doubt if any .person in the House is so prepared; but I think it desirable that a lien should .be given.

I would remind the minister of a very important case which changed the whole current of legal authority in Canada, as to the existence of the right of the Crown in respect of a provincial executive. This was the case of the Maritime Bank, in which case it was decided that the Provincial Government who represented the 'Crown had a first lien on the assets of the bank, and that the Crown was part of the Provincial Government, the

lieutenant-governor of each province being the direct representative of the King. By virtue of the general powers that existed in the Crown, the right of the Crown to its deposits in the bank was declared paramount over that of every other person. So that the Crown, as a matter of common law, has very special rights in advance of those held by any other person.
If a search were made in the Department of Finance, would that obviate the difficulty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) refers to a bank, but the Dominion clearly has jurisdiction there, because banking is one of the subjects in which exclusive authority is given to the Dominion.
The hon gentleman has not got my point. The Provincial Government had a deposit in the bank in question, and it was decided that the Crown, through the lieutenant-governor, had the first claim.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be in point; and to meet the case I would suggest that the word "first" be struck out. I think that would serve the purpose of the Act.

Does the Crown consent to come in after other lien-holders?
Sir THOMAS WHITE,; I would say so for taxes, and for a small amount. I doubt that it should come in against mortgagees, holders of mechanics' liens, and other similar charges. I move that in section 24, line 11, the word "first" be struck out.

I think the 'Grown has an absolute first right. I am not sure that the hon. minister is lessening the Crown's right in any way.
Section amended as proposed, agreed to.
On section 25-regulations:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These are regulations as to the district within which the board shall exercise jurisdiction and the places where they should sit and other matters relating to the proceedings of the board and to the general carrying into effect of the Act. Such a general section as this seems to be necessary to make the Act flexible.

The regulations, of
course, would be consistent with the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

266i

Will the minister make provision that this tax can be paid into any chartered bank in Canada to the order of the Receiver General or his department, so that the taxpayer will not have to remit to Ottawa and pay exchange?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That can be dealt with, if necessary, by regulation.

That is a reasonable
proposal, is it not?

speechtext:

On the schedule:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That in the schedule for incorporated companies, in form " J," the column, " cost of management, etc.," be struck out.

Is there anything to
be substituted, for it? How is the minister to arrive at the cost of management?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not really
necessary for the purposes of the Act. Tne gross profits and the net profits are shown. The difference would be the cost of the administration and the charges payable out of gross profits. I do not think the information as to cost of management will be necessary to the department in administering the Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Would it not be wise to have the column "money borrowed and debts due by taxpayers in connection with business," which is in the form for persons other than incorporated companies, also inserted in the form for incorporated companies? In making up a statement of persons or partnership companies, if you insert "the amount of money borrowed and the capital employed in the business," and add the two together, you havie the gross assets. It seems to me that a column with the same wording should be in the form for incorporated companies. I do not think there would toe any objection to dividing the assets in the case of incorporated companies by putting the capital stock in one column and then the unimpaired reserve, rest, or accumulated profits in another column, and the two added together would be the net capital in the business on which the tax' is to be applied. As ther.e is no provision made in the form for me liabilities of incorporated companies, it would be better to have a column similar to that for partnership companies. It seems to me
that the statement for the partnership companies is very plain, because, when you add together the capital and the money borrowed, you have the total assets, and then you have gross profits and net profits, which are taken from any ordinary balance sheet. I think the principle is practically the same in the case of incorporated companies, except that you could have the capital stock in one column and the reserves in another, and the two together, with the money borrowed, would make the total assets of the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is not necessary to make any change. My hon. friend will observe that in the schedule which relates to incorporated companies capital stock is shown; unimpaired reserve is shown; rest and accumulated profits are shown. All those together constitute the capital of the incorporated company, and all we need to know is the capital of the company and the net profits.
Why do you ask for the liabilities of a business firm and not those of an incorporated company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because, in order to get the capital of a business firm, you subtract the money borrowed from the gross assets. It may be necessary to insert in the business firm schedule another column showing the total value of the assets.
That would be a very wise thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But my hon.
friend will observe that there is power in the Act for the department to ask for other particulars, and it is possible that we may have to vary these schedules somewhat in the notices we have to send out.
It would be more convenient to the companies if the minister would make a separate column for unimpaired reserve or rest, and one for accum-lated profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will consider that when settling the form which we will send out.

The reason I make this
suggestion is that unimpaired reserve or rest is generally a permanent thing, and accumulated profits are carried to profit and loss account.

In the schedule for joint * stock companies, there is one column, "value of assets in Canada," and the nexfi

"value of assets outside of Canada." I would like to have some definition from the minister as to how a taxpayer, in filling up the schedule, should deal with stock which he holds in companies outside the bounds of Canada. Suppose he has stook in a company whose head office is in the United States or in Great Britain? Suppose he holds some of the Anglo-French loan among the assets of his estate? I would like the minister to give us a definition of assets outside of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is assets held by a company in respect of its business outside' of Canada. If I understand my hon. friend aright, he takes the case of, let us say, an American company that has a business in Canada and a business in the United States. In Canada such a company might have real estate, plant and machinery; it might have bills receivable; it might have stocks of Canadian companies. If such stocks were held in connection with its business, the assets in Canada would be the value of all such assets tha.t the American company had in Canada at that time in connection with its business here. Similarly, the assets of that company in the United States would be the assets in connection with its business there, whether they consisted of real or personal property or of stock. No doubt it will be difficult to ascertain precisely what is the amount of assets held by a non-Canadian company in Canada or held by a non-Canadian company outside of Canada, but we are not able to devise any better mode of arriving at the proper amount of the capital which we should take for the purposes of this Act of non-Canadian companies carrying on business in Canada. I admit that there is room for objection to the principle adopted, but I have not been able to discover any better principle than that of simply taking the assets in Canada and the assets outside of Canada, relating the one to the whole, and determining the capital of the company accordingly.

Is it the purpose of the minister to tax an income arising from assets outside of Canada? Suppose a taxpayer owns stock of the Union Pacific Railway on which he receives a dividend. The business of that railway, in which the taxpayer holds the stock, is not in Canada. Surely such concerns would be liable to taxation under this measure. Many of the large railway companies in this country own stock of railways outside of Canada that have no connection with Canada at all.
'Mr. Sinclair.]
Would the income derived from this source be regarded as part of the income which is assessable under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a Canadian railway company holds stock in an American railway company, and derives dividends from such stock, unquestionably those dividends would be part of the profits of the Canadian railway company, and would be considered in estimating its net profits for the purposes of this Act. Just as a Canadian business is assessable in respect of its profits, no matter whether derived from Canadian or foreign business, so a railway company holding shares in a foreign cora-pany, and deriving dividends therefrom, ' would be assessable in respect of those dividends.

Section 19, as to
appeal to the Exchequer Court, says:
The court shall hear and consider such matter upon the papers and evidence referred and upon any further evidence which the taxpayer or the Crown produces under the direction of the court and the decision of the Exchequer Court thereon shall he final and conclusive.
The Exchequer Court has no inherent power except what it obtains from the statute, and there may be nothing in the statute which gives it power to deal with this particular matter; consequently we have to come to this Act to find out what the powers of the Exchequer Court are under its provisions. In section 19, which purports to state what will take place when you get to the Exchequer Court, there is nothing to make the practice and procedure of the Exchequer Court specially applicable. I suggest' that after the last word in this section there might be inserted the words, " and the practice and procedure of the Exchequer Court shall apply to the hearing and decision of the appeal." This would give one more latitude in approaching a judge with regard to the question of taking the matter up in the province from which it might come, and would in other respects make the Acts more feasible and more workable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps it would be advisable to insert some words to meet the point that my hon. friend has in mind; it could be dealt with on the third reading. It may or may not be necessary to make the modification that my hon. friend suggests; the matter is somewhat complicated, and if we leave it until the third reading we -shall have time to consider it in the meantime.

On subsection b of section 3-dividends from tax-paying company exempted:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In reference to
this subsection, I am sorry that I am unable to concur in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). This subsection was inserted for the purpose of meeting the case of incorporated companies holding the stocks of other companies. If we widened the provision so as to include companies and individuals holding any interest in other businesses, difficulties would arise in connection with the administration of the Act, and I think there would be considerable room for evasion of its provisions. We have gone much further than is usual in the case of taxation measures of this kind in exempting holding companies in respect of dividends which they derive from the stocks of companies which they hold. After giving the matter careful consideration, I feel that we should not extend the principle so as to cover the cases of profits derived from other businesses by persons, firms and corporations.

I beg to move, by leave of the House:	'
That Rule 77 be suspended in reference to the Estimates presented this day in order that the same be considered in Committee of Supply this day.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Resolved, that towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenditures of the public service for fiscal year ended March 31, 1917, the sum of $99,458,597.41 be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should explain how this is made up. It was arranged with my Tight hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that there should be a vote of one-fifth in advance of the war appropriation vote, and it is made up in this way: The total amount to 'be voted is $132,501 -795,98 less deductions made in the House- I imagine these are items that have already been stricken off-of $63',414.50, leaving a balance of $1'92,438*,301.48. The amount already voted is 20,713,666.40. One fifth of the amount remaining to be voted is $20,744,931.01,. Adding these two amounts, we have a total of $49,458,597.41. One-fifth of the amount under the war appropriation resolutions is $50,000,000, which being added to the sum already mentioned makes the total of $99,458,597.41, the amount mentioned in the resolution.
I had not an opportunity of hearing anything about this before. Do I understand that this is one-fifth of the ordinary civil supply plus one-fifth of the war vote?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is composed of three items: first, the amount already voted; second, one-fifth of the amount remaining to be voted; and, third, one-fifth of the war appropriation.
To vote the war appropriation in Supply is a new method, but I suppose there is no objection to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I discussed that with the right hon. leader of the Opposition this afternoon, and informed him that according to the report of the officers of the House this was the only way in which it could be done.
I suppose it is, but when the War Appropriation Bill goes through will it be for the full amount?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I think it will have to be reduced by $50,000,000-one-fifth of the $250,000,000, which is the amount of the vote. The same is true of the other amounts.

The point I havie in mind is that the war appropriation is voted on a different principle from the ordinary Estimates. The responsibility for the administration of the war vote rests with the Government and; not with any one minister, whereas, in the case of the Estimates, the responsibility of the administration rests with the head of the department for which the money is voted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It will appear in the Bill in precisely the same terms as those set forth in the resolution. Further than that, it has been understood that these amounts are only to. he disbursed under Order in Council.

speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Indians, Ontario-relief, medical attendance and medicine, $11,000
Was the Big Chief up to see the hon. minister yesterday about this medicine?

From Prince Edward
Island. This is an item for relief to sick and destitute Indians who have no funds of their own and who. have practically to depend on departmental funds to provide them with the necessaries of life. The amount is the same as last year.

I have intended for several days to call the attention of the minister to certain things which have happened at Hagersville, Ont.
