I have received a letter from a merchant there complaining that the Indians, who are receiving bread from the Government, are not receiving the correct weight. If my hon. friend thinks it worth while to investigate this matter, I will send the letter to his deputy. The writer, who speaks on behalf of the Indians, Says that the baker is selling underweight bread.

There is no contract
entered into by the department at that point for the supply of bread. If the hon. gentleman submits the letter to me, I will look into the matter.

The minister is the
Indians' guardian in a way, and he is responsible for them. He should see that they receive the quantity of bread to which they are entitled. I will send the letter to his deputy.
Indians, Quebec-relief, medical attendance and medicine, $17,000.

My hon. friend was
kind enough two or three years ago to grant a certain amount towards the maintenance of a hospital at Caughnawaga. A French lady, Madame Perronot, who had certain means, desired, in the goodness of her soul, to consecrate her life to the welfare of the Indians. She had noticed that many of 'the Indians died at an early age, and she thought that, if she could supply a good hospital and if the Iroquois of Caughnawaga could receive proper treatment, she might save many lives. As a matter of fact, I think the department is aware that she is doing excellent work at Caughnawaga. She received at first just a pittance, and then my hon. friend very kindly increased the little indemnity. This year, however, on account of the war in France, she was not able to receive the amounts that she had been receiving in the past

from her family and her relatives, and she asked the hon. minister to increase the little indemnity. I think, if my hon. friend will have the hospital inspected and a report made of the work she is doing, he will reconsider the decision he took some days ago. This lady has given up all her revenues towards helping the Caughnawaga Indians, and it seems to me that the de-partmeht should do something to help her in that excellent work-

I quite agree with what
the hon. gentleman states as to the importance of this hospital and the good work in which it is engaged. I met the request that was made last year by increasing the grant by a couple of hundred dollars; but, in view of the fact that it was not our intention to increase any grants this year, I did not see my way to increase this one, and we thought it was rather sudden to have two increases in two successive years. The grant this year is the same as it was last year. I shall, however, be pleased to have the hospital inspected and a report made, as the hon. member suggests.
Can the minister tell me what portion of this appropriation goes into the county of Wright?
I cannot say off-hand, but I will get the information. The differentiation is not made -in the books here.
Perhaps the minister can tell me who are the doctors in attendance upon the Indians and what amounts they receive.

I will get the information for. my hon. friend a little later during the course of the evening.
Indians, Ontario and Quebec-repairs to ' roads and bridges and drainage, $21,900.
What is that for?

Certain roads and bridges
in connection with the various reserves require repairs and construction from time to time.
Do the Indians pay anything towards repairing their own bridges?

No. Usually we pay for
these through appropriations by Parliament. In some cases, however, the Indians make contributions which are supplemented by the provincial and Dominion Governments.

Could the minister tell
me if anything has been expended recently on the road at River Desert in the Maniwaki reserve? That road is every.year _ partially eaten away by the river Desert.

Yes, money has been spent on that road.
Indians, Nova Scotia-salaries, $6,200.

Who are the
Indian inspectors for the province of Nova Scotia?

Mr. Boyd and Mr. Foster are superintendents. The agents are: Mr. Hoyt, Annapolis; Mr. Harris, Digby; Mr. Freeman, Lunenburg; Mr. Chisholm, Halifax; Mr. Willis, Hants; Mr. Stephens, Windsor; Mr. Smith, Colchester; Mr. Johnson, Cumberland; Rev. MacLeod, Pictou; Mr. Cameron, Antigonish and Guysborough; Rev. Macdonall, Richmond; Rev. Mac-Pherson, Inverness; Dr. Sparrow, Cape Breton; Rev. Macdonald, Cape Breton; J. E. Campbell, Victoria; W. J. Whelan, Yarmouth; John Gibson, Shelburne.
Where is Mr. Foster located?
Halifax.

Do the^e men report to the minister with regard to the work they do?
Mr. ROCHiE: They report to the department -from time to time.
There is a report from Mr. Foster in the department, I suppose?
I presume so. All the superintendents make reports.
Is Mr. Foster devoting his time to this work just now?
I understand that Mr. Foster has enlisted.
What salaries are paid to these men?
$1,800 for Mr. Foster.

He is drawing his
salary now, though he has enlisted?
Yes.
What counties does he exercise supervision over?
Shelburne, Yarmouth, Digby, Annapolis, Queens, Lunenburg, Kings, Hants, Halifax, Colchester, Cumberland.
How many Indians are nnder him?
There is about an equal division of the Indian population, which amounts to some 2,000.
When did Mr. Foster enlist?
He enlisted prior to the first of November. J do not Temember what month. I think it was probably in August.

Is he drawing his
salary as Indian superintendent Us well as his military pay?
Yes, just the same as all other civil servants who enlisted prior to November 1.
Does the minister know what position he has in the military service?
No, though I believe that he is a lieutenant.
Who is doing the work in Mr. Foster's absence?
The other superintendent, Mr. Boyd, is doing his best to carry on the work.
Is there any fear of the situation being such that the other superintendent is being overworked, or that the minister would deem it necessary to appoint any one in Mr. Foster's place?
I have not heard any complaints that Mr. Boyd is not attending to his duties, and it is not my intention to appoint anybody to take Mr. Foster's place.
Last year when this matter was brought up the minister did not seem to know upon whose recommendation Mr. Foster had been appointed. Has he that information now?

I cannot charge my memory with who made the recommendation. I think I did explain last year that the appointment was made during my absence from the city by the acting minister. I do not really remember who was the acting minister at the time. I cannot tell the hon. gentleman on whose recommendation the appointment was made.

Is there any information in the department that would set forth the necessity for making the appointment, such
as a report that Superintendent Boyd was overworked and was unable to discharge his full duty?
Let us have the story. There must be a story behind it somewhere.

I am informed that the representations- that were made at the time were to the effect that we would get better service by the division of the counties between two agents than by having one superintendent cover the whole territory. That, I think, is about the only representation that was made.
From whom did this recommendation come?
As I told the hon. gentleman, I am not prepared to state that at present.

The minister was not prepared to state it last year either. When an appointment of so much importance as this is made, some justification for it should be given to the committee. Was Mr. Boyd unable to discharge his duties to the satisfaction of the department?

As I say, I do not think Mr. Boyd was unable to discharge his duties, but in the interests of the Service it was considered advisable by the acting minister, who made the appointment, to have a second superintendent, and that a division of the work would enable them to carry out the duties more efficiently than by having one superintendent cover the whole province. I -cannot tell, because I do not know, who made the representation.
Was it made in writing?
I presume so.
Is there any record of it in the department?
I presume so.

We are entitled to have this representation placed before the committee. Last year the matter was allowed to go by on account of a statement made by the minister that he was away and was not familiar with the circumstances. I think that he -should have familiarized himself with the circumstances by this time. Mr. Boyd lives in my county, about five miles from me. I know as a matter of fact that his duties as superintendent of the district to which he was appointed did not occupy all his time. His time was altogether at the disposal of the department, but the

duties did not take him away all the time, and I have never been able to understand what the necessity was for appointing him. I know that Mr. Foster had been secretary of the Conservative Association in the county of Halifax, and was very anxious to get an appointment from the Government, and so this appointment was given to him. It is a scandal in Nova Scotia that the appointment was made. The position is a sinecure created for Mr. Foster. The salary of $1,800 and expenses paid to Mr. Boyd has been doubled to Mr. Foster, and this at a time when we were at war. The appointment was made in October, 1914, when everybody knew that all the resources of the country would be required in order to enable us to bear the additional burdens necessary to carry on the war; but in the face of that a sinecure was created for Mr. Foster. He drew his salary from October until about the 1st of August, and then he enlisted and became a lieutenant. He is receiving his pay as lieutenant, but continues to enjoy his full salary of $1,800 as superintendent of Indian agencies in Nova Scotia. If the minister has any recommendation from any person which showed that it was necessary for him to create this new office and impose this additional taxation on the people, I think it right that we should know what the recommendation is and from whom it comes.
The hon. gentleman realizes that had I made the appointment myself and been in Ottawa at the time, I would have had a more distinct recollection of the circumstances.
That was a good excuse last year, but not now.

I am simply explaining why I have not a distinct recollection of the circumstances of the appointment. I am not endeavouring to escape responsibility for it. It was before the outbreak of war, in 1913.
I beg the hon. minister's pardon, the appointment was made in the month of October, 1914.
I think the hon. gentleman is incorrect. My information is that it was made in 1913.
Does the minister know if this official has performed any service since his appointment? Does he know of his doing one hour's work in the last two years?

He has sent in his reports, just as the other superintendents have done, as to the work that he is engaged in. 1 do not know of anything else on which we could depend. We insist on reports by all superintendents, and he has con-9 p.m. formed with that requirement like any other superintendent, and in these reports he sets forth just what work he has been doing.

Last year when the minister's Estimates were on the minister declined to justify the appointment of this man to this position. He said it had been made by the acting minister, as he says tonight, and of course, in a general way, he assumes responsibility for the appointment by the acting minister. But the statements last year by gentlemen on this side of the House with regard to Mr. Foster's appointment were of such a character that I am surprised that the minister did not, as a matter of duty-because I believe he is animated by some sense of duty-make some inquiry into the facts; and if he had made any inquiry whatsover into the facts he would have found that the appointment made in his absence was without justification, and an absolute disgrace to his administration. *There is nobody in Nova Scotia, of either party, who does not know it to be so. If the minister looked into it at all he must know that he has kept in office a person who is giving no value for the money he receives. It is a case of gross disregard of the common decencies of Government to permit the continuance in office of this man. Has the minister ascertained the date of the appointment?
There is no record here of the date of the appointment, but my deputy informs me that he is under the impression it was made in the fall of 1913.
I am under the impression, and I think my impression is very reliable, that it was in 1914-
You may be correct. I would not be personally sure.

-after the war was on, when there was no necessity and no justification for such an appointment. The fact that Mr. Boyd continued to discharge the duties of superintendent over the whole district for which he was originally appointed goes to show that there was no justification for Mr. Foster's appointment. It was a purely political appointment and nothing else.

The hon. gentleman knows that many men have gone to the war whose work is now being done by other officials, and that the same argument would apply to many members of the inside Civil Service who are at the front now, and whose work is toeing discharged by others.
(Mr. KYTE: I venture to say that there is no other case where an office was created after war was declared and the duties performed by a new appointee only for a few months, when a new person was appointed in his place. This situation is absolutely unique among all the instances of indefensible appointments in all departments of the Government.

What does the minister propose to do? It has been suggested that this officer has never yet performed any service, and I do not believe he has. He has enlisted, but I believe he is doing as much for the service, of the Indian Department as he ever did since his appointment. I do not believe he ever did one month's work, except that he revised the lists in Halifax county on behalf of the Conservative association. That is his business. He was not appointed because anybody additional was needed, or to perform any service. The work is not there for him to do, and he never intended to do anything when he got the appointment.
Does the hon. gentleman state on his own authority that Mr. Foster has never done any work?
Practically I mean to 3ay that. I have tried to find out what he has done, but I have never learned anything. He may have taken a trip once or twice out through the district.

I am quite willing to
bring down his reports.

I should like to see
them.

This item should
3tand, in view of the statements made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, not one of which has been questioned.
I have no objection to the item standing until the reports are brought down.

And also the recommenda-
' tions asking for the appointment?
I doubt if the hon. gentlemen would go so far as to ask me to dismiss this man because he has enlisted.
Certainly we do.
He should never have been appointed.

The minister need
not put forward the theory that because the man has enlisted-and we do not know whether he is in the home guard or for overseas service-
He is in the 112th regiment for overseas service.
Was that the first regiment he enlisted in?
I do not know.

I think my hon.
friend will find that he enlisted in some other regiment before the 112th, which has never yet been mobilized into proper shape. My hon. friend will be bound to admit the truth of the statements made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that this position was made for Mr. Foster, secretary of the Conservative Association in Halifax, who had to be provided for. The position was made without justification or excuse, and there was nothing for the man to do. We told the minister that last year. He knew it, and he has known it all along. He knew that when this item came up the matter would be brought before the House, and yet he has no defence to offer. So that because Mr. Foster, who has nothing to do to earn the $1,800 salary, goes and attaches himself to one of these numerous regiments that are being formed all over the country -and nobody knows when they will go to the front-we should not say anything against the appointment, is absurd. If the minister cannot show that the man has done something since his appointment to this position, and that there is something for him to do, which we deny, then the minister has no justification for keeping him in the employ of the department.	[DOT]
Is there a superintendent of Indian agencies in New Brunswick?
No.

It would be interesting if the House could get all the facts about these appointments, because there have been a great many in this department. The minister must not1 forget that his department has one of the worst records of any

of the departments. I do not say that it took place in the minister's time; it took place under his predecessor. I have an abstract' of a return made last year giving the number of appointments since this Government came into power in 1911, and the nurqber of dismissals in all the departments or in most of them. I find that the record of the Department of the Interior is as follows:	Since this Administration
came into power in 1911, there have been dismissed, 309; resigned, 374; and appointed, 1,651. So that Mr. Foster's case is only one of hundreds. I have no doubt that if we were able to get all the facts before the House it would arouse the country as to the condition of the Department of the Interior.

This is a separate branch, and has nothing whatever to do with the department of the Interior, but instead of an increase of hundreds as my hon. friends suggest, there have been only seven addi-tionaT officers appointed since the Government came into office. In five years' time, I think that is not a very bad record.
Who is the Indian Medical Officer at Baddeck, Victoria county?

Dr. H. A. Grant.
Mr. MACLEAN; Where does he reside?
At Baddeck.
Dr. Grant does not reside at Baddeck.

I am told that he resides at Whycocomagh, 12 miles from Baddeck.
, Mr. ROCHE: Yes, that is where he resides.

I think that Dr. Grant does live at Whycocomagh, just across the lake. There are no medical men left in the county of Victoria, and Dr. Grant lives nearest to this Indian settlement, and I suppose that it is for this reason that he was appointed. Hon. gentlemen opposite have expressed some doubt' concerning the circumstances which surrounded the appointment of Mr. Foster as superintendent of Indians. There was a little mystery about the appointment of a certain superintendent of Indians in the province of Nova Scotia, but it was not Mr. Foster; it was in connection with the appointment of another superintendent, Mr. Boyd. I understand that When he was appointed

some years ago there was a meTry little quarrel going on in the county of Richmond. There were two gentlemen who were ambitious to represent that county in the local legislature, Mr. Boyd and Dr. Bissett. The quarrel grew so warm that the party found it necessary to pull one of the contestants; off, and so he was appointed superintendent of Indians for the locality. He lives in an out-of-the way place, and perhaps he is not very wel! adapted for the office which he fills. But so far as Mr. F'oster is concerned, he is a young man, a man of education and of ability, and is admirably fitted for the post which he occupies.
Is he a good reviser of electoral lists?

If he devoted his attention to that kind of work he would be a good man. He is a lawyer of standing, and it requires a lawyer to look after that work, in Nova Scotia. Hon .gentlemen opposite do not know very much about the locality in which Mir. Foster performs his duties. I happen to live in that locality, and I know that he makes his visits regularly to the different reserves and agencies, and does his duty well. The fact that he has shown enough public spirit to volunteer for service on behalf of his country should not lay him open to this attack. I think it is very unjust. If, after the war, it should be found necessary to dispense with the services of one of these officers, I would say that probably the best thing to do would be to dismiss Mr. Boyd.
Oh, oh.

Perhaps it would noi
be necessary to dismiss any one, but if hon. gentlemen opposite are so exceedingly anxious to reduce the expenditure and to have somebody dismissed, I would say dismiss the older and less competent man.

With respect to the observations of my hon. friend from Annapolis, I may say that he is not as familiar with matters in my county as he used to be; he does not come so often. As regards the appointment of Mr. Boyd, he was appointed on the recommendation of the minister, and the fact that the Department of the Interior has found it necessary to appoint another person to take a part of his territory goes to show how efficiently and effectively Mr. Boyd has discharged his duties. The department has recognized that his

was a proper appointment. A superintendent of Indian agencies is so necessary in the Maritime Provinces that the department decided to appoint another, to have two instead of one.

I can hardly follow
the reasoning of my hon. friend, though it is somewhat characteristic. He says that, because it has been necessary to appoint another man to do the work which was supposed to be done by Mr. Boyd, that gentleman is competent. It does not seem so to me, and I think the people concerned in Nova Scotia are not satisfied with the work done by Mr. Boyd.

What does my
hon. friend know about it?

I know as much as my hon. friend from Halifax. He is the financial critic of the Opposition, but, so far as I know, he is not the Indian critic, and consequently I am inclined to take the view that I know as much as he does.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman is either thinking or saying. I understand him to say that the Indian affairs are very much better administered in Western Nova Scotia than they were because of the appointment of Mr. Foster. He seems to speak with personal knowledge, and I want him to tell the committee what he does know. Has he come in contact with the Indians, or visited the reserve?
I have an officer in the county of Annapolis who looks after the Indians for that county. I try to keep in touch with all my officials.
Hear, hear.

With all the officials who have been appointed on my recommendation. I think I have very efficient officials in Annapolis county, and I try to keep in touch with the public servants in that county. I know something about it; I do not pretend to speak about something I do not know. The other day the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) spoke about apple growing, and it afterwards developed that he did not know of the existence of a paper organized and run [DOT] by the fruit-growers of the Annapolis Valley and published in his own constituency. I hope I will not follow his example. I try to familiarize myself with any subject that I discuss.

Will the hon. member answer my question and not talk on side issues. Will he tell the committee what he knows about the manner in which Mr. Foster -performs the duties of his office? He seemed very anxious to do so a moment ago.

I stated that I knew of Mr. Foster's visitations, and of his consulting the official appointed in that locality. As a matter of fact, I think it is the duty of the hon. member for Halifax, who is making the charge, to give us the proof of his assertion.
I am not making any charge, but the hon. gentleman stated that he knew a great deal about a certain thing, and I want to find out if that is correct.

The charge was made
by hon. gentlemen opposite that Mr. Foster did nothing in connection with his duties, and I stated that to my -own personal knowledge he had made many visitations. I know from personal knowledge that the service is better performed by him than it was previously.

I want to help the minister out by voting this money, but so far I have absolutely no information about the service rendered by Mr. Foster. If the hon. gentleman knows, he ought to tell us what the service is that Mr. Foster has rendered. The minister was not able to tell us what service he has rendered. We cannot vote money to a man who has not rendered any service. Would the hon. gentleman please tell me what service Mr. Foster has rendered? What has he done? What are the visitations that the hon. member speaks about?
In so far as this item is concerned, I had been asked to let it stand, and I am not going to press it. I promise the hon. gentleman that I will bring down these reports.

I want to correct the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). He says that the reason this doctor, who resides at Whycocomagh, was appointed to attend the Indians at Bad-deck was that Whycocomagh is on the opposite side of the lake. The fact of the matter is that there is no lake between the two places. My hon. friend says also that the reason this doctor was appointed was that there are no doctors in Baddeck. The fact

is there are three doctors there, one permanently and two temporarily. I am not finding fault with the minister for getting a doctor in Inverness county, because there is no better doctor in Nova Scotia, but lest the people in that part of the country should read Hansard and see the remarks of my hon. friend and say that I was not paying proper attention to my business, I do not desire to allow his observations to go uncorrected.

It will be a surprise to the people of Nova Scotia, when they read my hon. friend's statement, to find that there is no lake Bras d'Oi lying between Whycocomagh and Baddeck. It will be news to them to learn- that Baddeck, is n^t upon a	lake.	My
authority for the statement as to the supply of doctors is Premier Murray, who made a speech in the Nova Scotia Legislature, as reported in that very reliable journal, the Halifax Chronicle, in which he stated that there were no medical men in the county which he represented and that as a consequence he'proposed to introduce a Bill to enable persons to practise medicine without complying with the ordinary requirements.
I cannot allow that to pass, because it is not true.
Premier Murray and my hon. friend from Inverness will have to fight that out.

There is no fighting about it at all; it is a matter of finding out who is right. There is a medical .doctor in Baddeck; in fact, there are two doctors there. Dr. Macdonald is now residing in Sydney, but there is another doctor-
Who is he?
Dr. Mclver. My hon. friend must know there is no lake between Baddeck and Whycocomagh. The fact is that Whycocomagh is 14 miles away from the reservation and Baddeck is right at the reservation.

Perhaps the hon. member for Annapolis will explain why a doctor from Baddeck was not appointed? Here is a man who resides right beside the Indian reservation. It would have been much preferable to have had a doctor right there to attend to serious cases.

Perhaps I was wrong, but if I was it was because I was going on the authority of the statement made by

the premier of the province. Perhaps that is rather an uncertain source of information, but when he made that statement I thought it was true.

The question of doctors having been brought up, the statement is made by my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) that the minister, when he wants a doctor for the Baddeck reserve, goes to Whycocomagh in another county. When was this Dr. Grant appointed?
About two years ago.
Does the minister know how far Whycocomagh is from the reserve at Baddeck? It is 15 or 18 miles.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The committee cannot possibly have a discussion unless there is some item before it for consideration.
We are discussing salaries.	*	[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item we have had under consideration is No. 286. This has been asked to stand.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked to have it stand and the minister consented.

I beg to express the opinion, speaking to the point of order, that you, Mr. Chairman, are wrong in regard to that. There are several items included in this general vote. It was understood that this item should not be finally passed until the minister gave us certain information, but that does not preclude us from taking up other items in regard to Indian affairs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is one other item before the committee, the item of $29,962. I do not wish to preclude discussion. I am in the judgment of the committee. I think I am right in saying that we should not discuss an item which an hon. member has asked to stand, but that we must proceed to another item if we are to comply with the rules.

That is not the practice of the committee. This resolution is subdivided into several items, and it has been the practice to deal with these items individually. I understand the minister to ask that the item for salaries stand for the time being. Surely it is in the interest

of the minister to get the other items passed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the request was only that the item of salaries stand the discussion is quite in order. My understanding was that the whole resolution was to stand.
I did not understand it in that way.

I am rather surprised at this attempt to restrict discussion. We were dealing with salaries, and it was understood that the item would not be passed until the minister gave us some information. But, before the item finally stands, we might give some further consideration to the question of medical aid. The question of why Dr. Grant was appointed two years ago, although he lives 12 miles away in another county, suggests to us the question why, in the county of Pictou, the minister dismissed Dr. Mackenzie, who had been attending the Indians at the Pictou Landing Reserve, as had been done by his predecessor while he was living in Pictou. The minister dismissed Dr. Mackenzie and appointed a man who lived in New Glasgow.

I understand that the hon. gentleman asked the same question last year, when the matter was fresh in my mind, and I gave him the reply. As far as my recollection goes, it was because the greater portion of the Indians resided nearer to where Dr. Grant lives in New Glasgow than where the other doctor lives. They reside just on the opposite side of the water. The major portion of the Indians reside on the opposite side of the water, and Dr. Mackenzie was in New Glasgow.
It is the other way round.

It may have been the
other way round, but at any rate it was by reason of the representations that .were made at the time that he was appointed. It was pointed out to me that Dr. Grant's appointment would be more convenient to a greater number of the Indians than that they should be attended to by Dr. Mackenzie.

Of course, the whole thing was a little piece of politics; that is the cold English about it. Perhaps the minister might explain why Dr. Grant of Whyeocomagh was appointed instead of one of the doctors at Baddeck. We have heard suggestions about the peculiar con-168
dition that has developed through the country as to the deficiency of doctors. There was no such deficiency when Dr. Grant was appointed to look after the Indians in another county.
It had not struck me that Dr.. Grant lived in another county; he lived in the county in which New Glasgow is.
I am speaking about Dr. Grant of Whyeocomagh.

This appointment was made, as the other appointments were made, no matter what Government was in power,-on the recommendation of those in authority who have the recommendation in their hands, and of those in whom we have confidence. T'he representations made were such as convinced me that it would be a wise appointment and a convenient appointment to be made, so far as attending the Indians is concerned. There was nothing exceptional in this case.
Dr. Grant was appointed to succeed Dr. Macdonald?
Yes.	'
W'ho resided at Baddeck?
Yes.
Why was he dismissed ?
I explained why the other man was appointed. I cannot carry all these things in my head two or three years after the appointment was made.
Partisanship5
I do not know.

I desire to ask the minister a question for information, with regard to a matter which does not relate exclusively to his department, but which has come up this evening. The question is as to the salary of the civil servants who have enlisted. It is extremely unfortunate, I think everybody will agree, that the anomalous condition should exist that some civil servants who have enlisted are in receipt of their salaries while others who have enlisted are not. I am not going to discuss that as a matter of policy, but I think the Government is open to very grave censure for not continuing that policy, or else for having established it at all. I do not know that we have ever had any explanation from any minister as to why that policy was emibarked upon. But



surely it is very objectionable to see special favours extended to some men who enlisted prior to others. How does the Government justify it? It cannot be based upon any sound principle surely-to say that the man who enlisted before the 1st of November shall 'be entitled to his pay, whereas the man who enlisted a few days later shall not. The question I desire to ask for information is this: Suppose that a man enlisted a week before the passing of the Order in Council in November, but was not actually attested-I think that is the word; he did not sign the roll-until a day or two after the passing of the. Order in Council, would he be entitled to his salary?

In all such cases the official produces the certificate of his superior officer, and we are guided by that certificate as to the date. Prior to the 1st of November, 1915, of course, we were paying thfe salaries of all officials who enlisted, and they were allowed their military pay as well. I have explained this all before, and I think there is not a minister whose Estimates have been before the committee but has been called upon to deal with it. I can only repeat that we are paying only the difference between the military and the civil pay. Some take the ground that we should have instituted that originally, but I do not know of any who have taken the ground that we should continue it, even though we found the payments made such a large drain on the war vote, because the substitutes of these men, when they have substitutes, are all paid out of the war vote. We are doing no injustice to those who enlisted later than the 1st of November, for all knew in advance exactly what the conditions were. We could not tell how long the war was going to last; by many it was not thought at first that it would be so protracted, nor did we think that we should have such a large number enlist as have enlisted. But when so many were enlisting, and the war continued so long, we thought it well to relieve the strain on the war vote, and that we should revise by Order in Council the rate to be paid.

I know many who enlisted with the idea that they would get their full salary. They resigned or abandoned their official work before the passing of the Order in Council, and, perhaps, in many cases, actually were in uniform, but did not happen to make the attestation or signature of the roll until a time subsequent

to the passing of the Order in Council. Many mem enlisted thus expecting to get their full .salaries, but they did not sign the roll early eneugh, and were not able to get their full salary.

I understood the minister to say that substitutes in the departments were paid out of the war vote. Where can we find out just what amount from the war vote goes to the different departments to pay for substitutes?

I think that information
was laid on the Table of the House some days ago.
Item stands.
Indians, New Brunswick, $16,284.
What is the Indian population of New Brunswick by divisions?

The total Indian population is 1,862. The number of reserves is 26.
I will send the hon. gentleman the report of the department which gives in detail the information he asks for.

Thanks; if it is in the
report ,1 can read it up. What is the total amount of salaries paid, say in the last fiscal, year?
To whom was the money paid and in what amounts?

The list is as follows: John
B.	Sheridan, $800; B. J. Griffin, agent, southwestern division, $500; N. J. Wooton, agent, northern division, $350;. constables at Big Cove, $20; constables at Burnt Church, Northumberland county, $50; constables at Eel Ground, Northumberland county, $24; unforeseen services of constables, timber guardians, etc., $190; amount to provide timber inspection in the Red Band reserve, $50; total, $1,984.
When was Mr. Sheridan appointed?

He was appointed quite
recently to take the place of his predecessor, who had died.

Can the minister give
me anywhere near the exact date of the * appointment?
Last autumn.

That is as near as the
minister can come to it?
Yes.

When was Mr. Wooton appointed? I may say before that question is answered that I observe in the Auditor General's Report that the name of the officer for the northwestern division is given as Mr. Waite, and I was very much surprised to learn of the change. I know both these gentlemen,' and Mr. Waite is a very fine old gentleman who has lived in that portion of New Brunswick all his lifetime. I can vouch for the fact that he was probably much more in need of the salary than was the person who was appointed in his place, and I think he is just as good a Conservative as the present incumbent1. It was somewhat of a surprise to the people in that district to learn that the change was made. Mr. Waite is not one of the bad Grits, because they turned that fellow out and put Mr. Waite in his place. We expect that sort of thing to happen; but why Mr. Waite was put out and the other man put in his place is somewhat of a mystery. As the northwestern division is in that portion of the province which will be joined to the county which I now represent, I naturally have a little curiosity to know why these changes have taken place.

If my memory serves me
right, the bon. gentleman was not so enamoured of the services of Mr. Waite last session as he apparently is to-day. If he will read Hansard, I think he will find that he made some severe strictures upon Mr. Waite.

I think the minister will search in vain for any public record of any strictures that I made upon Mr. Waite. I think I had a private conversation with the minister about Mr. Waite, but I do not think I made any strictures upon him. I rather pitied him. I think I told the minister that he was in the hands of a pretty bad outfit, who were forcing the poor old Indian agent to do things that he ought not-to do. Other than that, I have no knowledge of ever saying anything against Mr. Waite, and he is the last person in the county of Victoria that I would feel like making charges against. If anything irregular took place I am sure it was not the fault of Mr. Waite; it was the fault of the men who were behind Mr. Waite, compelling him to do what he ought not to do. Will my hon. friend tell me the reason of the change?

Complaints were made
about the manner in which Mr. Waite rendered his services, and we had an officer go to that division and report, and, as a re-168-1
suit of his refort against Mr. Waite, we considered he was not discharging his duties efficiently or to the satisfaction of the public, and therefore we relieved him of them. There was nothing political in the matter, as the hon. gentleman knows. It was solely and wholly by reasons of representations made to the department that he was not giving efficient service that he was relieved.
Will the minister allow me to be a little personal and ask him if he is relying upon the conversation I had with him?
Nof at all.

I am glad of that, because the last thing I had in mind was anything that would militate against Mr. Waite. I want to repeat in the most public manner possible that, while I think Mr. Waite may have been induced to perform certain services in a manner not entirely in the public interest, yet I do not for a moment blame Mr. Waite, I blame the men who were behind him and who were profiting by Mr. Waite's perhaps somewhat easy method of carrying on public affairs.
My hon. friend knows there was one mat-, ter to which I referred in this House. I* do not know that I discussed it. I asked a number of questions, and, after a good deal of persistent boring, I got the information; and after I got started, I found no disposition on the part of the minister to withhold the information to which I was entitled. I refer now to the attempted steal of practically all the lumber on the Tobique Indian Reserve. Fortunately, through the active and energetic efforts of the Rev. Father Ryan, who has charge of the Indians on that reserve, it was prevented. As I have said, I have no fault to find with the minister; in fact, I think he is entitled to a great deal of commendation for the energetic manner in which he prosecuted. I understand he was up against a pretty stiff proposition in the shape of a man who was always looking out for himself, and who had the matter well planned. Had it not been that the minister was firm in the matter, the Tobique Indian Reserve would have ceased to exist eo far as any lumber was concerned.
I was, however, anxious to know whether the statements that I had made to the minister regarding the Indian agent at that time had anything to do with his dismissal.

and I am very glad to knew from the minister that I am not the cause in any way of Mr. Waite's losing his position. I regret that he - has lost it, because, after all, these positions as Indian agents in New Brunswick are all mere sinecures. No one ever thinks for a moment that an Indian agent earns his salary. I do not suppose an Indian agent really earns $50 a year, because there is nothing for him to do. He travels around amongst the Indian reserves once in a while. There are only a few of them, with perhaps a dozen Indians1 scattered around in a little encampment, and when they get hard up and want some flour or pork, they send for the Indian agent and he goes and gives them what they require, It seems to me to be a hardship that this Mr. Waite, who really needed the money, was fired out of the position, and the real, active, energetic head of the Conservative party in the county of Victoria was placed in it. The man who was appointed there is the man who, for a time, ran the newspaper, and who monopolizes all the little party funds that were going. He is after everything that has money ih it, and he seems to have been successful in landing this position for himself. I have heard-I do not know how true it is-that even this man has got into trouble and has also been fired. I hope that is true, but I am afraid there is no such good luck as that. I would like the minister to say whether that is true or not.

I think the hon. gentleman is doing an injustice to the present incumbent of the office when he states that he is so very fond of grasping the finances that he has landed this job for himself, because, as a matter of fact, he did not seek the job at all. In fact, he has wanted to resign the position.
I have heard that.
But he has not been dismissed.
Has he resigned?
If he has sent in his resignation, it has certainly not been accepted.
Will the minister state whether he is any better satisfied with the way in which the present incumbent is managing his honorary duties than he was with the services rendered by his predecessor?

I have not had any complaints that would lead me to believe that

his services are more satisfactory than those rendered by Mr. Waite. Of course, he has not been very long in the position as yet. Every agent will no doubt make mistakes; he cannot please everybody.

Is the minister aware of the fact that within the last three months some 800 or 900 acres of land in this reserve were put up for sale? The most important lumbering firm in New Brunswick applied to this agent for a description of the land; they wanted to cruise it and see what was on it. The agent refused to give the representative of this firm the information- wrote him a letter and told him that he did not have it. Not until after the tenders were opened in Ottawa was the information given to the party who wanted to cruise the land and tender for it. When representations were made to the minister's department the sale was cancelled and new tenders called far. Afterwards tenders were received which were mudh higher than the one which had been recommended; by the minister's agent. Is the minister aware of these facts?	.

The action to which the hon. gentleman has referred was taken by my order, and instead of being impliedly criticized toy the hon. member, I should be commended. The hon. gentleman states that tenders were called for a certain piece of land. That is very true; a tender was received. It is true, also, that another lumber firm had written to our agent asking that he might be instructed as to where the land was in order that he might cruise it and put in a tender. Through oversight -or some other reason, I know not-he did not get the information until the tenders had been opened in Ottawa. When it was brought to my attention that this gentleman did not have the information, although it had been promised by the agent, I immediately instructed the. Deputy Superintendent General to call for new tenders, which resulted, as the hon. member intimated;, in the receipt of close on to $500 more for the land. That shows that the minister and his officials are anxious to conduct this department in a fair and impartial and honest manner. I am not going to say that Mr. Wooton, the agent who overlooked notifying this lumber company, did so designedly. I am not in a position to say that, but no matter whether he did or not, the matter has been pointed out to him and the explanation has been afforded. In fact, it has reached our ears.

also, that this lumber company had found out what the original tender was, which accounts for the new tender being $400 or $500 higher. At any rate, we showed our desire to have everythlimg conducted in proper manner by calling for tenders for the second time. It was represented to me that it was a strong political friend who put in the first tender and a strong political opponent who put in the second one, but the highest tender was accepted.

If the minister will allow me, I again congratulate him for the manner in which he has conducted the affairs of the department so far as he is concerned. I want to say here that I think the minister has acted with the very greatest regard for the public affairs of his department in this particular case. If he will refer to my remarks in Hansard to-morrow, I think he will observe that I found no fault with his department; in fact, I am endeavouring to commend the department. I am only pointing out some of the things they have to contend with down in the province of New Brunswick.
Politics are very strenuous down there.

Perhaps it may surprise the minister when I tell him that I have no warmer supporter in my constituency than the gentleman who put in the first tender. Both parties were Liberals, and very active ones at that; so the minister is wrongly informed about the politics of the gentleman who put in the first tender. Would the minister think that I was impertinent if I were to ask him if the incident to which we have been referring is the cause of Mr. Woofon's desire to retire from the position?

No, I believe not-not to
my knowledge.

When was Mr. .Griffin
appointed, and where was he to reside?
J am afraid that I am not in a position to givie the dates of those appointments, as I have not any record of them here. I can give, the information later to the hon. gentleman.
T suppose he takes the place of a Mr. Smith whose name I find in the Auditor General's Report?
Yes.

The minister has given
me the date of Mr. Sheridan's appointment -and thereby also hangs a tale. Hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia seem to think that they have a grievance; that politics have played a part in the appointment of a man by the name of Foster in that province. I wonder if the hon. minister is aware of the circumstances connected with the case of Mr. Sheridan? It may surprise the minister when I tell him that for some years previous to his appointment Mr. Sheridan had been a member of the legislature of New Brunswick and that in the month, I think, of April last, on account of very serious charges that had been made by the Opposition, a royal commission was appointed, ostensibly with power to investigate many matters in the province of New Brunswick, among them the expenditure of certain road moneys in different counties. In the county of Kent an investigation was held by Mr. Chandler, who was the commissioner, in which it was proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that this Mr. Sheridan had been party to absolute theft of public moneys of the province of New Brunswick. It was established that Mr. Sheridan's son, a boy of twelve or thirteen years of age or thereabouts, was placed upon the pay-roll in connection with certain public works. It was shown that this boy was not on the works at all; that the cheque was made out and delivered out to the father. When the superintendent who had been responsible for this was put upon his oath, he said: Mr. Sheridan had been pretty good to me and I wanted to help him all I could. Therefore they made out these bogus payrolls and bogus cheques, which were endorsed by a person other than the boy, and the money was drawn from the treasury of New Brunswick. Mr. Sheridan was obliged to get out of public life in New Brunswick on account of practically pilfering public money from the province. The very moment it was found that this man was not fit to be a member of the legislature of New Brunswick he was handed over to my hon. friend the minister who appointed him an Indian agent under the Federal Government at a salary of $800 a year. The matter complained of in Nova Scotia was only a matter of taking $1,800 a year out of the treasury of Canada, but this case is worse. It is almost compounding a felony. It is giving a position in the public service to a man who got kicked out of the Legislature of New Brunswick. The Lord knows they are kicking them out pretty faist down there. Another fellow was fired the day before yesterday for boodling:	1
i

do not know whether my hon. friend will *find a position for him for boodlirig-for taking money that did not belong to him. He has been found guilty by the same royal commission; I hope my hon. friend will not find a place for him. How in the world can the minister justify the appointment of this man Sheridan under the conditions that I have stated? Perhaps he did not know the circumstances; if so, he ought to find fault and make some one explain why a man of this kind was foisted upon him. If he did know, then I must say that I have not the same high regard for njy hon. friend that I have had in the past and that I want to have in the future. Nothing that has happened in my province since the famous investigation which resulted in the resignation of the premier has cast such a discredit upon public life and has caused people to wonder if there is any such thing as honesty in public life as did the appointment of Sheridan to the position of Indian agent, having regard to the revelations made before the royal commissioner. I do not know who recommended him; I suppose it would be the member for the county of Kent (Mr. Robidoux). It is in the county of Kent, and I have no doubt the member for that constituency will assume responsibility for the appointment. But it reflects very little credit upon whoever appointed him, and I hope the minister will be able to tell this committee that he did not know the condition of affairs, and did not know what was happening when this man was appointed.

As to the accuracy of the statements that the hon. gentleman has just given the House, I know nothing. As the hon. member will realize, a minister, in making appointments throughout the country, cannot know all the conditions of the different appointments.
I appreciate that.

I do not know who Mr. Sheridan is. He was appointed in the usual way. If we have a representative from that constituency supporting the Government possibly the recommendation may have come from him. The vacancy was kept open for some time, and the nomination of this gentleman was accepted in the usual manner. I certainly heard nothing against Sheridan's character in line with what the hon. member has said to-night; it is all news to me. Possibly if some other member from New Brunswick, conversant

with all the facts, were present to-night he might be able to put a different colour on these statements.
No, he cannot do it.
At any rate the hon. member will appreciate that I was not in a position to judge of the character of Sheridan, and in such a case a minister must be guided by the recommendation of his friends.

I appreciate the position, and I am glad to know that the minister was not aware of the conditions, because I wish to repeat that since the present minister took charge I have found nothing on his part or on the part of his officers but a desire to administer the department properly. I wondered if the Hon. Mr. Roche could be aware of the condition of affairs when this appointment was made. He says that possibly if some other gentlemen were here he might throw a different light on it. I did not know that the matter was coming up to-night, or I would have armed myself with the report of the Royal Commission. It is a public document, which was published in the newspapers of New Brunswick two or three days before Christmas, and if the minister wants to get the facts he has only to send to the library for the report. Mr. W. B. Chandler was the commissioner. He is a lawyer of high standing in Moncton, of such high standing, indeed, that when they tried to throttle him and not allow him to go on and investigate, he resigned rather than be made a cats-paw by any political party. But he had gone far enough to investigate Sheridan and a man named Stewart, the late member for Gloucester in the New Brunswick Legislature. The report is a public document, and in it the minister will find every statement I have made. In fact I have been very modest, and not made my statement as strong as it might have been made. I am surprised that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), who must have known something of the appointment, did not inform his colleague of the true position of affairs before the appointment was made. It may be that the member for Kent, who is new in public affairs, who has not had much to do with public matters, possibly may have thought that he could put one over on the minister without being caught at it. But that is not the case with the Minister of Marine, because he knows the

game in New Brunswick from a
10 p.m. to z. I say again that I am surprised that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not inform his colleague of the true condition of affairs, that he was appointing a man who, on the1-report of a Royal Commission, would have to resign or be kicked out of the legislature of New Brunswick. The same condition of affairs existed with regard to the other man, Stewart. Stewart would not resign; he hung on and met the legislature. The Government of which he was a supporter refused to appoint him on any committees. The newspapers took the matter up. Stewart would not resign, and sat in the legislature for four or five weeks. Finally a resolution was moved, about a week ago, asserting that he was not a fit and proper person to hold a seat in the House of Assembly. The Government took the ground that the motion was improperly brought, that there was no jurisdiction, and in some way virtually whitewashed him. But public sentiment became so strong that two or three days ago, I see by the newspapers, he resigned. J hope to the Lord the minister will not give Stewart a job. It is bad enough to give one of them a job. I hope that the Minister of the Interior will report this matter to his colleagues, and see that Stewart is not given a position, as the other fellow was. They were both proven guilty of the same offence by the same commissioner, and were equally bad. It is truly a disgraceful condition of affairs, and I can only say again, I am heartily glad that the Minister of the Interior did not know the conditions when he made the appointment.

The hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) has referred to a recent appointment to the position of Indian agent in the province of New Brunswick, in the person of Colonel Sheridan. He has given the committee some information with regard to this man's standing, and some reasons why he should not have been appointed to the position he now holds under the minister. I should like to supplement the hon. member's statements, because this man took good care not to resign, and held his seat in the legislature until he had received the appointment from the Department of the Interior to the office he now holds. I had a conversation with this man quite late last autumn, and while newspaper rumours had it that he had been appointed Indian agent in the room and place of the - deceased officer, Mr. Irving, he said he was still debating whether or not he would
accept the position. The truth is that Commissioner Chandler's report had not been given to the public at that time, and he was not sure whether he would have to get out of the Legislature or not; he was awaiting that report before accepting the appointment at the hands of my hon. friend. My hon. friend says that he had no intimation in regard to this man's reputation or character before he made the appointment. I do not know what principle the ministers follow in regard to getting information concerning appointees, but ii does seem to me that, in the province oi New Brunswick at least if they get mo information they tumble on the very worst class of citizens in making appointments and Sheridan is no exception to the rule.
I have here the report of the Auditor General for the year ending March, 3il, 1916. I notice that Mr. Irving's salary is paid only to the 30th of November, 1914. At the same time there is a Mir. Hutchison who received two months' salary. 1 presume he was acting for the two months from the 1st of February to the 31st of March. Apparently there were two months in the year when no salary was paid for an Indian agent in that division of the province of New. Brunswick. Is that correct.

This gentleman did the
work as acting Indian agent until the appointment of Sheridan was made.
, Mr. COPP:	Until the appointment of
Sheridan?
That cannot be.
That is what I say-I cannot understand the report. I am reading from the report up to the 31st of March, 1915. Mr. Sheridan was not appointed until late in the fall, November or December, 1915.
Mr. Irving was paid for eight months until November 30.
Of what year?
1914, and then Mr. Hutchinson acted for two months until the 31st of March, the end of that fiscal year.
Why was he acting?
Some time elapsed before an appointment was made.

When did Mr. Irving die?
iMr. ROCHE: In 1914, before Christmas, I think.
I think the hon. minister is mistaken. Mr. Irving died last year.
I met him in 1915.
I travelled with him in the summer of 1915.
Yes, it was 1915.

This report gives the appointment down to March 31, 1915, but it shows that Mr. Irving got his salary for only eight months. He was certainly Indian agent until the summer of last year or the fall, perhaps till September, though I do not know the exact date, and I cannot understand why be received only eight months'. salary and why Mr. Hutchinson came in.
I understand that for some time before Mr. Sheridan was appointed there was no agent at all.
That might be, but why did Mr. Hutchinson come in?
I must frankly admit that I do not know anything at all about it. I do not know when the man died, and my deputy cannot give me the information offhand. I will get it later on for my hon. friend.

I shall be glad to have the information, because it struck me as a rather singular matter. I could understand Mr. Hutchinson coming in a year later and acting as agent until it was known whether Mr. Sheridan was going to be forced out of the Legislature. Mr. Hutchinson may have acted for a couple of months until the investigation concerning Mr. Sheridan was concluded. There is another matter with regard to which I should like some information. I notice that the province is divided into three divisions, and I think the minister told my hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) that there were 26 reservations in the province, Can he tell me how these reservations are divided, and the number of the Indian population in the three divisions?
In the northern agency the number is 224, in the north-eastern agency 939, and in the south-western agency 533.

I thought that the northern division was somewhat smaller than the others, and I was surprised to notice in the Auditor General's Report that the fees of the doctors in other portions of the

province are somewhat small compared with those of Dr. Peat who was paid $400 for attendance on the Indians in the smallest division.

It is true that Dr. Peat got $400, but there are others who got $200, for instance, Dr. Coleman and Dr. Leger. Dr. Arnold got $150, Dr. Desmond $300, Dr. Gorman $300, Dr. McKeifzie $200, and Dr. Gilchrist $200. Several of the others got $150 and $175.

But Dr. Peat got the largest salary, though he has the smallest district. I should like to ask, also, how the provisions are supplied to the Indians. Are they purchased 'by the agent's orders whenever he sees fit and wherever he sees fit? Are they purchased by tender, or how is it done?

The local agent sends in a requisition to the department for the amount of provisions required for the particular Indians that he superintends, and he is authorized to make the purchases at the best prices.
If an application is sent to him, does he go to the place and ascertain whether the party applying sells what is required?
That is what is expected of him.

In my county there is a small reservation where the Indians work. They have quite a little farm, and yet I see certain amounts charged. I see there is a doctor's bill for $150, although there cannot be over a half a dozen families on the reservation.

I would like an assurance from the minister that he will bring down the papers wljioh I have asked for before the close of the session. I know there is not much use in asking that this item stand, 'because we are getting near the close of the session, and probably when these items come up again it will be about two or three o'clock in the morning and they will go'through. Will he give me an assurance that he will bring down all the correspondence with reference to the appointment of Mr. Sheridan to the position of Indian agent?
I shall have no objection whatever to bringing down any correspondence on file. I have no recollection of any particular correspondence but such as there is I will bring down.

While it may be too much to ask the minister to remove this man from office if he finds that what I am saying is true, I would like at least to aek if he ydll not get some of the officials of his department to look up the report of Mr. Chandler, which he will find in the newspapers of New Brunswick about the 21st or 22nd December last, and see if he does not come to the conclusion that this man ought not to be an Indian agent or to hold any position in the Government of Canada. When a man has so conducted himself that he is not fit to be a member of the Legislature of the province, he is not fit to be an agent looking after the expenditure of the money of this Government. My hon. friend, while I gladly say that he was perfectly innocent in this transaction, is not elevating the standard of public life in Canada very much when he is rewarding a man of this kind under the conditions which I have indicated. While I do not know that I can ask thfe minister to say offhand that he will dispense with the services of this man, I think I have a right to ask that he will give the matter his very serious consideration and, if he finds the statements I am making are correct, that he will seriously consider the advisability of dismissing this man from the public service. I am making no attack upon Mr. Sheridan, I am only discussing him now because he has been found guilty by a public commissioner, a gentleman appointed by his own political friends, and I do think that the minister will be doing something in the way of trying to purify .public life in our province, which, I am sorry to say, has reached a pretty low ebb, by removing this man from his position and removing him from the public gaze where he remains as an incentive to other men to go and do wrong because it seems that in our province the greater the wrong a man may commit the greater the reward he gets for his services. I think the hon. gentleman, as one member of this Government, should take a firm stand and show the people that every thing politically 'is not bad and miserable in this country although that seems to be the way things are drifting in New Brunswick. I can only ask the minister to give very careful consideration to this matter.
I will inquire into it.

I want to express my sincere regret that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) saw fit
to leave this chamber just before this item was brought up. I think we should have a statement from him as to why this man was appointed, and why he should have allowed his colleague to be drawn into the position that he finds himself in to-night. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is hot doing himself credit by absenting himself from the chamber at a time when he ought to be here to defend his conduct.
Indians, Prince Edward Island, $3,225.
When was the assistant superintendent appointed?
About two years ago.
There was no need for his appointment. It is just that much additional expenditure. Where does Dr. Stewart live?
Tyne Valley.
There was no necessity for Mr. Arsenault's appointment.
Was not Mr. Arsenault the old agent? He got very old and the superintendent Rev. J. A. Macdonald, was appointed to do the work.
Mr. Arsenault was appointed two years ago.

He was an old official of
the Government.

No, he may be a man of the same name but he is not this man.
' Indians, British Columbia, $182,650.

Before entering upon
the consideration of this item, I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior if he has any papers, correspondence and reports which he could give to us in reference to the Kitsilano reserve in Vancouver which has been purchased by the British Columbia Government. The circumstances connected with this reserve are exceedingly peculiar and are such as to demand consideration from this committee. The Government is the trustee of the Indians. It is its duty to guard the rights and property of the Indians just as it is the duty of any trustee to guard the interests of his trust. In the case of this reservation, there was a property belonging to the Indians worth, by common consent, between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000, a very valuable property situated in the city of Vancouver, on the south side of False creek. It occupied a position which was of strategic im-

portance in connection with the entry of railways into Vancouver. Among other railways which were desirous of getting into the city was the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul, one of the large American companies. That property was acquired by a person who had been expressly or impliedly set to work to negotiate with the Indians, and it was obtained f*220,000. I think the correspondence, which the minister will find on file, will show that this Government, or the Department of Indian Affairs, were aware of the negotiations which were going on with the Indians, and I think it will be admitted that it was the duty of the minister to intervene and see that the highest price which it was reasonably possible to obtain for the Indians was obtained, or to see that the interests of the Indians should not be unnecessarily sacrificed. The fact that there were comparatively few Indians represented, that the property was of enormous value and that the Indians would receive, even at the price which was paid, quite a large amount of money, is no answer for this Government to set up for neglecting to discharge its duties as the trustee for the Indians. It was its duty to obtain for the property what it was fairly worth. My information is that the amount actually paid the Indians was $220,000.
I find on examination of the records of what took place in the British Columbia Legislature, that there was read a telegram sent by Mr. Bowser, Attorney General of British Columbia, to the Minister of the Interior at Ottawa, stating that the purchase could be made for that sum. But, strange to say, the British Columbia Government actually paid $300,000; and of that sum, the enormous amount of $80,000 was paid as commission on the transaction. Some very interesting proceedings have taken place in the British Columbia Legislature and also in the courts of British Columbia, in a case which was brought on appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and judgment given, and in which the court makes very severe remarks in regard to payment of this very extravagant commission. It would appear that the deal was put through by Mr. Read, a clerk in the office of the firm of the Attorney General, the firm of Bowser, Reid & Wellbridge. Mr. Read, the clerk to whom I have referred, had some connection, it appears, with Mr. Alexander of Winnipeg. After negotiation with the Indians, an option was obtained in the name of Mr. Alexander. It appears, from an examina-

tion of the witnesses before the committee of the British Columbia Legislature, that first the option was taken in the name of Mr. Read, but afterwards, for reasons not explained-whether it was because Mr. Read was the clerk in the office of Mr. Bowser's firm-I do not know-it was changed from the name of Mr. Read to the name of Mr. Alexander. And when the $300,000 was finally paid, it was paid to Mr. Alexander and went through him, and he handed over to Mr. Read the very large sum of $39,000 as a share of the profits or commissions on the transaction. It does not appear that Mr. Read had done anything to earn that $39,000, and when he was asked before the committee what was the consideration for which he had received this amount, his only answer was that he thought he had earned the money'-although he admitted that he had done practically nothing for it-that Mr. Alexander was a man of honour and had paid him this amount of money as a man of honour would do. These are rather extraordinary facts. I do not know whether the Minister of the Interior has had his attention called to the matter or not, but he must have correspondence in his department bearing on the subject. But I think that before the item goes through the committee should have such details as are available to the minister. I am not going into details in connection with the matter, hut these are the facts to which I have referred: first, that the property in question was worth between $1,000,000 and $2,000,000; second, that this Government was informed of the negotiations which were taking place and the property was purchased for the British Columbia Government for $300,000; and, third, that the $300,000 did not go to the Indians, but the sum of $80,000 was paid out as commission to those who carried through the transaction. I would ask the hon. minister to give information to the committee with regard to the transaction, and to state what steps, if any, the Government took to safeguard the rights of the Indians.

I will say a few words with reference to the question put by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), and the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), a local man, who is acquainted with the facts, will go into the matter more in detail. It is true, as the hon. gentleman has stated, that the Provincial Government of British Columbia did make an arrangement with the Indians on the Kitsilano reserve to surrender their reserve for $220,-

000, or something in that neighbourhood. The Legislature of British Columbia did vote $300,000 to close out the deal. The negotiations with the Indians were carried on in much the same manner as those in the surrender of the Songhees reserve were carried on. There, also, a viery large commission was allowed. In this case, if anything wrong has been done with regard to the reserve by the Provincial Government they are amenable to the people of British Columbia. But the Government of which the h'on. member for St. John was a member did not hold themselves responsible for the commission paid to a Mr. Matson, or some such name, of about $75,000, in connection with the Songhees reserve. I think the hon. gentleman is astray when he speaks of a telegram sent to the Minister of the Interior.
In the investigation before the committee reference is made to a telegram from Mr. Bowser, the Attorney General, dated March 17.
In what year?
The year in which the transaction took place, which, I think, was 1913. I take my facts from a newspaper report of the evidence.
There was no telegram sent to the Minister of the Interior. That telegram, as I read it, was supposed to be sent to the Hon. Mr. Rogers, after he had ceased to be Minister of the Interior.
How long has the present Minister of the Interior been in office?
Since the 1st of December, 1912. I think the telegram referred to some conversation had with the then minister. No telegram was sent to me as Minister of the Interior.
It is said that it was sent to Mr. Rogers when he was Minister of the Interior.

In March, 1913, he was not Minister of the Interior. This Government did not authorize that dealing and did not confirm it. And the best evidence that we have not been satisfied with the arrangement with the Indians by the British Columbia Government is the fact that to-day we are arranging, on the recommendation of the Royal Commission that have investigated the matter, to have this property disposed of to the Harbour Commission of the city of Vancouver, and the sum the
Indians will eventually get out of it will be the sum that is determined by expropriation proceedings on the part of the Harbour Commissioners. Therefore, it is not only $220,000 that the Indians will eventually receive, but it will also be the excess amount over that which, upon investigation by arbitration under the Expropriation Act, the Harbour Commissioners will pay this Government. The Indians, of course, will get the benefit of all of that excess.
Against whom are the Harbour Commissioners expropriating?

They are expropriating the reserve, dealing with the Dominion Government on the report of the Royal Commission, which made a recommendation to this Government that we should dispose of the reserve to the Harbour Commissioners and allow them to develop their harbour properties there, and they have the authority [DOT] under an expropriation clause in their charter to expropriate this Kitsilano reserve.
Expropriate as against the Dominion Government?
Under the Indian Act and the expropriation provision that they have in their own charter.

Do I understand that the property, which the Indians- are supposed to surrender unless this arrangement that was made with the Government, will be valued by arbitrators, and the difference between the $300,000 and the total value ot the property be put into the funds of the Indians?
That is the agreement

As I have some rather intimate knowledge of this matter, the committee will perhaps bear with me for a moment. I may say at the outset that this Government has at no time officially recognized the action of the Provincial Government in acquiring the reserve. It does not follow, however, that the Provincial Government were entirely wrong in their, action. I think they were actuated by a desire to solve a problem which had been concerning the people of Vancouver for many years, that is, how to get rid of this Indian reserve in the heart of the city. As nearly as I member the circumstances, the Provincial Government had an intimation that the Indians were ready to deal, and they thought it would be a good opportunity for them to take action.

It must be remembered also that the provincial Government claim reversionary-rights. I also understand that the Government of Canada has never officially recognized the reversionary rights of the provincial Government and that it is a disputed point that has never been determined by law or by agreement. During the last couple of years the Indian Commission, a joint commission between the two Governments, was appointed for the purpose of solving the dispute, if one might call it so, between the two Governments, relating to all Indian reserves. When the Provincial Government took the action that it did, I strongly opposed it on the ground that this particular reserve should be kept for public purposes, for the public of Vancouver or for the Harbour Board, which at that time was not constituted, or for the city itself to administer. There was a friendly difference between myself and the provincial authorities whose sole Object was to take advantage of the willingness of the Indians to sell in order to get rid of them, just as happened in the case of the Songhees reserve. In taking the action which they did, they followed, as the minister has pointed out, the precedent of the Government of which my hon friend is a member, and they employed the same methods exactly of carrying it out. As to the value, of this reserve, the hon. gentleman says it is worth from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000.
I did not say that; I say" that is my information.

The value of the reserve depends a great deal upon certain things. If the reserve carries with it the ownership of the foreshore butting on the reserve, that adds to its value; but, as a matter of fact, the Indians have simply riparian rights, and that does not carry with it ownership from the 'Crown of the bed of the harbour, so that that detracts a great deal from its value.
Another point is this, that before this reserve can be utilized for waterfront purposes, it will cost a very large sum to build a breakwater at the western side of the reserve jutting into English bay, and that also must be taken into consideration, because of the value which my hon. friend has mentioned is a value based upon what the reserve may be worth used as a harbour property, and it cannot be used as such until such action is taken as I have mentioned, that is, the

securing of the ownership of the foreshore and also the construction of the breakwater. That question, however, will all be settled by the Board of Arbitration which has been appointed. The Government of the Dominion, in all the negotiations relating to this reserve, have at all times acted strictly in the interest of the Indians. They have refused to recognize any action which is not in accordance with the Indian Act and of the statutes of Canada, and in the interests of the Indians financially. The Board of Arbitration will be completed and will commence its work, I think, in the near future. The Harbour Board, under the powers given to them in the Harbour Act, have the right to expropriate, and in the Indian Act, there is a clause which provides for expropriation for public purposes.
