Under these two powers the process of expropriation is being carried out. An offer has already been made to the Indian Department by the Harbour Board of something like half a million dollars, but it has been refused by the department as inadequate, and that has made it necessary to carry on the expropriation proceedings and to appoint a Board of Arbitration to settle the matter. The matter will be settled in a manner which will be perfectly above board and in the interest of all concerned.

What title did the
British Columbia Government obtain from the Indians, and how, if they have any title, could the Harbour Board expropriate their rights unless there was some special power to expropriate against the Crown as represented by the British Columbia Government.
The Indians have absolutely no right to give title to any one except under the provisions of the Indian Act.

The British Columbia
Government have paid $300,000. Of that amount they have paid $220,000 to the Indians and $80,000 in commissions to Mr. Read and Mr. Alexander. How can the rights of the British Columbia Government, whatever they are, be expropriated by the Harbour Board? The Provincial Government must think they have some legal rights or they would not pay $300,000.

The British Columbia
Government claim reversionary rights, and the determination of the value of those reversionary rights will be done by this arbitration.
Is the British Columbia Government a party to this arbitration?

Yes, a consenting party, and it will have counsel present although it has no member on the board. I think it was last June or July that the Provincial Government agreed to become a party to the arbitration. That practically answers the questions raised by my hon. friend, other than this that he mentioned in his remarks that Mr. Read and Mr. Alexander were authorized. He, of course, meant authorized by the Provincial Government and not by this Government.
By the Provincial Government. I thought I made myself clear.

I also wish to make this point clear in fairness to the Provincial Government. The hon. gentleman pointed out that Mr. Read was a clerk in Mr. Bowser's office. At the time this deal was put through, Mr. Read had left the employ of Mr. Bowser, and has not been in his employ since.

Was that R. L.
Reid?
No.
This was a gentleman named Hamilton Read, who was clerk in the office.

He was a young lawyer from the Old Country, who was really clerk in the office, but he was not clerk at the time this deal was consummated, nor has he been since. That ought to be stated, in fairness to the Attorney General.
The record shows, as a matter of fact, that he did not leave until the very day that the $300,000 cheque was issued, March 31, 1913.
If the record shows that, I cannot dispute it. All I know is that at the time the deal was closed he was not and since then has not been in the employ of Mr. Bowser.

This report-it is a newspaper report, and may not be correct- states that Mr. Read was with Mr. Bowser's firm until March 31, 1913. Then, later on, it. says that the deal was closed on March 11, and that a cheque was issued for $300,000 on March 31. So that at the time the deal was closed he was clerk in the Attorney General's office.
I think that is incorrect, and in justice to Mr. Bowser's firm that ought to be made clear.

It was charged in the provincial election.
Mr. .STEVENS: I know. Without any question, he was an employee in the office when the first steps were taken regarding these Indians, but he left the employ of the firm before the deal was closed. In fact, there were two or three deals and one or two fell through before ,the deal was finally closed. Mr. Alexander, who closed the deal, is a stipendiary magistrate, a man of very high standing.
He was, I think, the first child born in Vancouver; he knew all the Indians, and it was his acquaintance with them that enabled him to make the deal. I have no comments to make on the commission that was alleged to have been paid, or as to the right of the Provincial Government to take the action it did, other than to say this: they were actuated originally by a desire to get rid of the Indians. For many years this question had been vexing the people of Vancouver. The heart of the city was a poor place for an Indian reserve, and it was very desirable that the reserve should be closed. The outcome will be distinctly to the advantage of the city of Vancouver, of the public and of the Indians themselves. A very much larger sum will undoubtedly be secured and placed to the credit of the Indians in the department here. I think that the Kitsilano deal, from the Dominion Government standpoint, is a highly creditable transaction. I am not speaking of the provincial end of it at all; the Provincial Government are responsible for that; they must take the responsibility, and I assume that they are willing to do so. Sq far as this Government is concerned, and so far as the negotiations authorized by this Government are concerned, they are of a very proper type.

What I object to is not the action of this Government, but their inaction; their doing absolutely nothing to guard the rights of these Indians. They must have known that these negotiations were going on and that the rights of the Indians were being purchased for an amount far and away below their value. They should have taken steps to protect the interest of the Indians in this respect.

The hon. gentleman
must remember that the Provincial Gov-

ernment was acting entirely on its own responsibility. The Prime Minister of Canada repeated time and again on the floor of the House that this Government had never authorized or recognized the action taken. That is on Hansard.

If the Provincial Government has any right in the reserve it is because the Indians ceased to occupy. This Government allowed the Provincial Government really to put the Indians off the reserve, tear down their buildings and so make them absentees from the reserve, bringing into operation a law, if it 'be the law, that would give over that reversion of interests to the British Columbia Government. And this Government stood idly by, they being the trustee for the Indians, bound by a sacred duty to protect their rights, and allowed them to be dispossessed of their rights in that way. I am very glad, indeed, that it has been determined to leave the matter to arbitration and that there shall be paid for the benefit of the Indians what the land is worth. But it does not seem to me that the fact that the Indians will be likely to- get what their land was worth is the result of the very widespread and very strong agitation which took place in the city of Vancouver.
Not at all.

There has been a good deal of agitation there; it would seem as if the Government had been forced to move. My complaint is that at the time that the interests of the Indians were being sacrificed, this Government, knowing -that such was the case, stood idly by and allowed this to go on, just the same as a trustee might stand by -and see the property rights of the cestui que trust taken away from him. I do not think that the Government is free from blame for not intervening at that time. If a private individual or company had done what the British Columbia Government did in reference to these Indians, and the Government was aware of the fact, surely it. would have been its duty to intervene and protect the rights of the Indians. The fact that it was the British Columtoia Government that was despoiling these Indians, moving them from the reserve and tearing down their buildings, does not in -any way alter the situation. With regard to Mr. Bead, I have here a report of the proceedings of the Legislature, in which it is stated that the cheque was issued on March 31, 1913, and that

Mr. Read h-ad then been for some time a clerk in -the office of the Attorney General's firm, and remained with the firm until that day, the 31st of March. The Attorney General had apparently been informed that the Indians could be bought out for $220,000. When I referred to the matter I thought that my hon. friend the present Minister of Public Works was Minister of the Interior at the time, but it appears not. The telegram was to Hon. Mr. Rogers, dated March 17. This is important only as showing that this Government knew, through one of its ministers, that these negotiations were going on with the British Columbia Government. It was then the duty of the Government to intervene and see that the rights of the Indians were protected. It shows, also-, the extraordinary fact that the Attorney General of British Columbia, although he then knew that the Indians were willing to take $220,000, coolly handed over to Mr. Read, who was then, or had been, clerk in the office, and to Mr. Alexander, the very large sum of $80,000 as a commission for something which Mr. Read evidently was not able to put any value upon. There appears to be no adequate consideration for any such exorbitant commission as that. My hon. friend seeks to justify it.
No, I do not.
Yes.

No; I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I stated that for whatever action the Provincial Government had taken they would have to foe responsible to the people of British Columbia. I made no comment on its being either right or wrong.

Does not my hon. friend see that on this valuation the British Columbia Government will .claim back the full sum of $300,000, not merely the $220,000 which was paid to the Indians, but also the $80,000 which was thrown away? Necessarily that will be recouped to the British Columbia Government out of the amount which these valuators, or arbitrators, may allow, and to the extent of that $80,000 the Indians will toe deprived of that which they ought to have got; because it seems to me a most outrageous thing that, for the services of Alexander in getting a few Indians, not more than 20, to sign an option, there should be paid the very large sum of $80,000. When the arbitration instituted by this Government is

concluded, this money must necessarily come out of the Indian fund. .
Not necessarily.

Yes, because the British Columbia Government will say: "We paid $300,000 for the purpose of getting these titles; it could not come from any other person, and the British Columbia Government would be entitled to get it."
My hon. friend is putting up a plea for the British Columbia Government.

No, I am stating the
fact.

You are interpreting the
result of the arbitration.

I do not. know whether the arbitrators will allow half a million dollars or a million and a half dollars, but out of whatever they do allow, the British Columbia Government will have that recouped to them.

My hon. friend forgets
that the British Columbia Government has reversionary rights.

It has no reversionary
rights or rights which come into operation until these Indians left their reserve. But here the Indians were allowed by this Government to be turned out of the reserve by the British Columbia Government. The British Columbia Government burned down their buildings and induce them to leave their property, and it would be by virtue of that act and that act alone that the reversionary title under the law would become vested in the province of British Columbia.

Does my hon. friend
know what buildings they burned down?

I am told that there
were a number of Indian shacks, not very important. But the Indians as a rule do not live in palaces, and I presume it was a very easy thing for the British Columbia Government to expel the Indians in a night and have all the shacks removed quickly, and no doubt it was done quickly. The British Columbia Government, by reason of the Indians having left the reserve, assert their rights under the law, claiming that these rights thus became vested in British Columbia. Here is what is said with regard to price: One witness states that he asked Mr. Read how much the reserve was
worth and Mr. Read told him from one to two million dollars. Then, with regard to Mr. Read's services, he said his share was $39,525. This question was put to him:
Q. You did pretty well for one who had nothing to do with the deal?-A. Yes.
Q. The Attorney General didn't engage you, nor did Alexander. What did you do for Alexander to earn this $39,000?-A. Nothing. Alexander did what any honourable man would do. I suppose he admits a moral obligation like some people do.
So that for doing absolutely nothing, rendering no service of any value whatever, except to draw an option in his own name which he afterwards changed to read in the name of Mr. Alexander, this gentleman, Mr. Read, a clerk in the office of the Attorney General'e firm, received the very large sum of $39,000, and that $39,000, even if this arbitration results in some further amount to be paid to the Indians, must come out of the funds to come to this Government, because the British Columbia Government paid out the amount and they, I presume, will have no difficulty in inducing this Government to believe that they acted bona fide and ought to be recouped for whatever amount they have actually paid out.
My hon. friend referred to the Songees Reserve. I know nothing with regard to that, but I should say, myself, that if it appeared to this Government that any gentleman had been treated as Read was treated by the British Columbia Government, we would think that conduct very censurable indeed. Whatever was done in regard to the Songees Reserve, is no justification for this very indefensible transaction, so far as the British Columbia Government is concerned. As I said, the only respect in which I blame this Government is for their inaction, shutting their eyes and permitting this indefensible thing to go on under which the Indians' rights were sacrificed, while this Government took no steps to prevent that being done.

There are one or two corrections that I must make to the hon. gentleman's remarks. Apparently he has got the impression that a considerable number of the Indians were forced off the reserve. As a matter of fact, this reserve was used by the Indians as a sort of lodging place or camping ground when they visited the city. I do not think that more than one or two of them stayed there for any length of time, but numbers of the band used to come over there and stay for short periods. They have three other reserves

in the vicinity of Vancouver, and lived on these reserves and not on the Kitsilano.
I also wish to disabuse my hon. friend's mind of the suggestion that this Government has done nothing. There has been in connection with this Indian reserve one of the most difficult problems to solve that the Indian Department has had to deal with in the last three years, and I can assure the hon. member that they have done a great deal indeed. If they had not done a great deal we could not possibly have brought the matter to such a successful issue. They have arranged for a settlement, in a large degree, of the differences between the Dominion and the Provincial Governments. The whole question has been considered by the Royal Commission, and took a great deal of time. The procedure of expropriation 'by the Harbour Board has all been carried out step by step legally, which also took a great deal of time. Ever since the day that news arrived that some action had been taken by the Provincial Government, there has been the utmost activity on the part of the Department of Indian Affairs to reach a proper solution, and I can assure the House and my hon. friend that not only have the Government not been derelict in their duty, but they have been very diligent indeed in protecting the interests of the Indians, and the outcome should convince my hon. friend of that fact. He misunderstands the action of the Provincial Government. ' It is based upon a claim put forward by them in their own right, and not as friends of this Government or as acting on behalf of this Government. This Government contends, I contend from what I have seen of the case, that their claims are not well taken in every sense. Some of them are, but most of them are not, and they have at last come to see eye to eye with this Government. The hon. member is certainly not justified in condemning this Government for inactivity during this transaction.

I have not complained ol inactivity since the transaction closed, I say the inactivity was during the transaction, and while this wrong was being done to the Indians. During the last year or two, since public opinion has been aroused in the matter, I think the department has been acting with considerable diligence.
It was referred to the Royal Commission long before that.

It was their duty to take steps to right, as far as they could, the great wrong which had been done to the Indians. They are entitled to the large sum of $80,000 which was wrongfully taken from them, and which will in all probability never be restored to them.

From time to time they have made interim reports, but they have not yet closed their work entirely. I expect, within the next six weeks, or at most by the middle of May, to receive their final report.
There has been no report presented to Parliament in (connection with the matter.
No.

commission has made interim reports from time to time, and that these reports have dealt with specific matters.

question that was referred to this Royal Commission to start with?
I suppose the hon. gentleman refers to the duties that were assigned to the commission.
Yes, there was some main question that was assigned as the reason for the appointment of the commission.

I might read one of the clauses under which the commission have been acting:
Until the final report of the commission is made the province shall withhold from preemption or sale any lands over which they have a disposing- power and which have been heretofore applied for by the Dominion as additional Indian reserves or whioh may during the sittings of the commission be specified by the commissioners as lands which should be reserved for Indians. If during the period prior to the commissioners' making their final report it shall be ascertained by either Government that any lands being part of an Indian reserve are required for right of way or other railway purposes, or for any Dominion or provincial or municipal public work or purpose, the matter shall be referred to the commissioners who shall thereupon dispose of the question

by an interim report, and each Government shall thereupon do everything necessary to carry the recommendations of the commissioners into effect.
The hon. gentleman no doubt knows that the British 'Columbia Government have laid claim to the reversionary interest, but the Dominion Government could. give no clear title to any of those Indian lands, and any one disposed to purchase them would have to go to the province to get a quit claim.

As I understand it, the real question was the ownership of the lands in the various Indian reserves in the province of British Columbia. The province claimed that they were the owners of those lands whereas the Dominion Government claimed that they had some right to them in the same way as they have the right or fee to other lands in western Canada. Of course, other questions have arisen in connection with the lands in the province of British 'Columbia; they may be on a somewhat different basis than the lands in other parts of western Canada. But what troubles me about the matter is not so much the question that is before this commission, as the time that it has taken to arrive at any conclusions. What the commission has been doing, I do not know. I saw reports in the papers a couple of years ago about it travelling in different parts of British 'Columbia. I do not pretend to know as much about their duties as the commissioners themselves, but it seems to me that the question to be determined was a purely legal question.
They visited every reserve, and there are 1,100 or '1,200 reserves.

I know that there are a good many reserves, but what information could the commission get with respect to the legal ownership of lands, with respect to determining whether these lands were vested in the province or in the Dominion, by travelling to the reserves?
It was to determine whether or not they had enough land, and to enlarge and reduce the reserves as well.
These duties must come under some other clause than that which has been read.
I read only one clause.

Supposing that this commission wanted to investigate every Indian
in the province of British Columbia, I fail to see why they should have taken from the 12th of April, 1913, until the 7th of April, 1916, a period of three years, to carry out their investigation. There are a number of men on this commission. I do not know very many of the members personally; I presume they are well qualified. I see on the list the name of a former member of the Saskatchewan Legislature, L. H. Mac-do wall; the others I do not know. But when I look at the amounts which have been drawn from the public treasury by these men in three years, I feel certain that they would stagger the ordinary citizen in this country, particularly when he considers the money that has been spent, not only on this commission, but on other commissions appointed by this Government. I find in Hansard, on page 2144, answers to a question asked by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) with respect to this commission, and I see that up till the 29th February of this year Mr. N. W. White had drawn $29,545 out of the public treasury, Mr. J. P. Shaw had drawn $29,430; Mr. L. H. Macdowall, $29,730; Mr. S. Carmichael, $20,790, and Mr. J. A. J. McKenna, $22,663.76, or a total up till 29th February, 1916, of $273,367.64. It is only fair to say that the Dominion pays only a portion of that amount, but the proportion to be paid by the Dominion up to the 29th of February, 1916, is $154,722.23. It seems to me that that is a tremendous amount of money to be spent on an investigation of that kind, particularly as the main question at issue was a question of the ownership of those lands, and a question that could be determined just as well by the commission sitting in the city of Victoria or Vancouver as by going to the Indian reserves throughout the length and breadth of British Columbia. The ordinary Royal Commission consists of only one man, sometimes of two or three, but here we have five men on this commission, drawing princely salaries out of the treasury of the Dominion Government, and, I submit, not doing very much to earn the money. It seems to be another instance of extravagance on the part of the Government, and I am sorry that it is located in the department over which my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior presides. We have heard a good deal of criticism of that department, and I think it only fair to repeat that there are a great many more employees in it to-day than are needed to perform the public service at the present time. The



minister has- stated that he expects .a full report from this commission in a very few weeks. I hope that his expectations in that respect will 'be realized, and that we will have an end of this commission and have the question decided finally before very long.
